items.title: RustGIS
items.text:
A fast, free and open-source GIS in pure Rust for mapping, analyzing and sharing geospatial data.

RustGIS runs natively on Windows, macOS and Linux, and in your web browser. Your data stays on your machine unless you send it to an AI model you choose, and every action is a command you can script from the command line, a notebook or the AI Assistant.

Try it in your browser Download Get started Compare

items.title: Highlights
items.text:
• Your data, any map

    GeoJSON, CSV, Shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, KML, GPX, GeoTIFF and cloud-optimised GeoTIFF, web tiles, vector tiles, PMTiles, MBTiles and MapLibre styles, drawn on a 3D globe or in any projection, on the desktop and in the browser; STAC catalogs, Overture Maps, OpenStreetMap, open-data portals and S3 buckets; SQL, DuckDB and live PostGIS databases on the desktop. Data · Formats · Maps

  • Cartography

    Unique values, graduated colours and proportional symbols, collision-free labels, effects, extrusion, page layouts, map series, reports and presentations. Cartography · Layouts

  • Analysis

    SQL selection, overlay and proximity tools, guided workflows, ModelBuilder, imagery tools and over 1,000 GeoLibre and Whitebox tools for terrain, hydrology and LiDAR. Analysis

  • Editing

    Create and modify features with snapping and templates, keep attributes valid with domains, subtypes and rules, and undo anything. Editing

  • AI Assistant

    Ask about your data or tell the map what to do. The assistant runs RustGIS commands with the model you choose, and every change can be undone. AI Assistant

  • Scriptable and extensible

    rustgis-cli and the rustgis Python package run any command by id, render maps and chain tools; the MCP server lets AI agents make maps; sandboxed WebAssembly plugins add commands, tools and ribbon tabs. Command Line · Python · MCP Server · Plugins

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
RustGIS is a layered Cargo workspace. Lower layers never depend on the UI, which keeps the engine scriptable and the front end swappable.

Layer Crate Job L0 rustgis-geom Coordinates, extents, Web Mercator, geodesic distance/area, scale L1 rustgis-data Features and typed attributes; GeoJSON, CSV, Shapefile; a read-only SQLite file reader (sqlite, for GeoPackages in the browser); data providers reading GeoPackage, GeoParquet and FlatGeobuf in place by their spatial index, and PostGIS tables live (desktop) (GDAL formats and DuckDB queries converted by those programs when installed); SQL where clauses; rasters (GeoTIFF, ASCII grid) and their coordinate systems L2 rustgis-map, rustgis-analysis Layers, symbology, labeling, camera, basemaps and web tile layers; geoprocessing tools L2 rustgis-tiles Web map tiles: XYZ/TMS/WMS raster tiles, Mapbox Vector Tiles, PMTiles and MBTiles archives and a subset of MapLibre styles; a cache that fetches in the background (worker threads natively, the browser's fetch on the web) L3 rustgis-render tiny-skia renderer, label placement, PNG export L3 rustgis-geolibre The GeoLibre tools as geoprocessing tools: run by the optional geolibre program natively, by geolibre-rust's WASI runner in the browser L3 rustgis-plugins Plugins: sandboxed WebAssembly modules that add commands and geoprocessing tools; .rgplugin packages and the plugin registry L4 rustgis-engine Session, undo, command registry, sample project L5 rustgis-assistant The AI Assistant: a chat agent that acts through commands; OpenAI-compatible, OpenAI Responses (a ChatGPT plan's sign-in), Anthropic and Gemini wire formats as plain request/response data, so the desktop (a thread), the browser (fetch) and the command line share one loop L6 rustgis-ui-egui The ribbon front end apps rustgis, rustgis-cli, rustgis-web Desktop app, command line, browser (WebAssembly)

items.title: Everything is a command
items.text:
Each user-visible action is a CommandSpec with an id, label, ribbon location, shortcut, parameter description, an enabled check and a run function. The ribbon, keyboard shortcuts, command search and CLI all dispatch through Session::run, which also snapshots the project for undo and restores it if a command fails.

Plugin commands (plugin:<plugin>/<command>) dispatch through Session::run too, as one undo step. While they run, they reach the session only through permission-checked requests (see Plugins).

items.title: Never crash
items.text: Production code avoids unwrap, expect and panics, and treats file contents and command parameters as hostile. Tests run every command and every geoprocessing tool with junk parameters.

items.title: Quality gates
items.text: cargo xtask ci        # fmt, clippy -D warnings, tests, layering check

items.title: Command Line
items.text:
Every ribbon action is a command with an id. rustgis-cli runs them headlessly.

rustgis-cli commands                  # every command id with its parameters
rustgis-cli tools                     # geoprocessing tools
rustgis-cli info data.geojson         # layer summary as JSON
rustgis-cli render data.geojson map.png --basemap ocean --width 1600 --height 900
rustgis-cli render data.geojson map.png --tiles 'https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png'
rustgis-cli logo icon.png --size 256  # the app icon as a PNG
rustgis-cli plugins                   # installed plugins (also: browse, get, install, uninstall…)
rustgis-cli skills                    # the AI Assistant's skills (also: add, remove, enable, disable)

items.title: Chaining commands
items.text:
run loads data or a project, runs --cmd 'id={json params}' in order, and can save the result:

rustgis-cli run --sample \
  --cmd 'gp.run={"tool":"countPoints","params":{"polygons":"Countries","points":"Cities"}}' \
  --cmd 'layer.symbology={"layer":"Countries_Summarize","type":"graduated","field":"point_count"}' \
  --cmd 'bookmark.go={"name":"Europe"}' \
  --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"europe.png","dpi":192}' \
  --save atlas.rgis

Each command's result goes to standard output as JSON. What a command says beside it, which the app shows in its status bar (a file's warnings, or that only the first 32 tables of a GeoPackage were added), goes to standard error.

Installed plugins load first (--no-plugins skips them), and --plugin <file or folder> loads one more for this run only. Their commands and tools have ids like plugin:vector-toolkit/hexagon-grid:

rustgis-cli run --sample --plugin vector-toolkit-0.1.0.rgplugin \
  --cmd 'gp.run={"tool":"plugin:vector-toolkit/hexagon-grid","params":{"input":"Countries","size":300}}' \
  --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"hexagons.png"}'

Rasters work the same way:

rustgis-cli render dem.tif dem.png
rustgis-cli run --data dem.tif \
  --cmd 'raster.symbology={"type":"shadedRelief","ramp":"Terrain","zFactor":1.5}' \
  --cmd 'raster.info={}' \
  --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"relief.png","dpi":192}'

items.title: Asking the AI assistant
items.text:
ask gives the AI Assistant one request. It loads data like run, then the model answers and acts on the project through commands; --save keeps the result:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=…            # or OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY
rustgis-cli ask --sample "Which 5 countries have the largest GDP?"
rustgis-cli ask --sample "Buffer the cities by 200 km and label them" --save buffered.rgis
rustgis-cli ask --data parcels.geojson --provider ollama --model qwen3:8b "Summarise the fields"
rustgis-cli ask --models --provider openai          # the provider's models
rustgis-cli ask --login                             # sign in with ChatGPT to use your ChatGPT plan
rustgis-cli ask --sample --provider chatgpt "Zoom to Tokyo"

The provider is --provider (anthropic, openai, chatgpt, gemini, openrouter, ollama, custom), else RUSTGIS_ASSISTANT_PROVIDER, else the first with a key in the environment, else Ollama (a ChatGPT sign-in is used only when chosen). --model and --base-url override the defaults. The answer goes to standard output and each command the assistant ran to standard error. Commands that read or write files or use the network are declined unless you pass --yes; plugin commands, scripts, tasks, models and replacing the project are always declined here. --trace log.txt appends each request and response body (never the headers, which carry the key) to a file. --login signs in with ChatGPT in the browser, so --provider chatgpt uses your ChatGPT plan (--another-account registers RustGIS for a different account), and --logout signs out; see Signing in with ChatGPT.

items.title: Serving AI agents
items.text:
mcp runs RustGIS as a Model Context Protocol server for agents such as Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code, which then run commands, look at the map and search the documentation themselves:

claude mcp add rustgis -- rustgis-cli mcp --sample

See MCP Server.

items.title: Contributing
items.text:
Contributions are welcome. See AGENTS.md for the conventions.

  1. Fork the repository and create a branch.
  2. Make your change with tests. New behaviour is a command in crates/engine/src/cmd/.
  3. Run cargo xtask ci and pre-commit run --all-files.
  4. Open a pull request. CI runs on Linux, and the docs build a preview. A maintainer can label it ci:windows, ci:macos or ci:full to test those platforms before merging; main and the nightly run test all three.

items.title: Test data
items.text: Generate small datasets during tests instead of committing fixture files. The shared generator in tests/support/ogc.rs builds OGC landing pages, collection lists and GeoJSON in memory; tests/support/ogc_server.rs serves them locally for engine and UI tests. The sorting smoke test similarly generates its KML, KMZ, CSV and GeoJSON inputs. These run automatically with cargo test --workspace --locked and cargo xtask ci, without a separate setup step or a public service. Extend these generators when adding cases.

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
The site is built with Zensical:

pip install -r requirements_docs.txt
zensical serve        # http://localhost:8000

Images live in rustgis-assets and are linked by URL; don't commit images to this repository.

The screenshots are rendered by the app itself. crates/ui-egui/examples/shots/render.sh runs the ui_shot scripts beside it and writes WebP files to target/shots/; copy them to images/ in rustgis-assets. The assistant shot asks a real model, so set an AI Assistant provider and key first (see AI Assistant).

items.title: Releases
items.text:
1. Bump version in the workspace Cargo.toml and merge it.
  2. Run the Release dry run workflow, which checks the version and builds every package without publishing anything: gh workflow run release-dry-run.yml -R opengeos/RustGIS --ref main -f version=<version>
  3. When it passes, publish a GitHub release tagged v<version> (the tag must match Cargo.toml).

The Release workflow then builds and attaches the Windows installers, zip and MSIX, the macOS DMGs, the Linux tarballs, .deb and .rpm packages and AppImages, and SHA256SUMS. To try the packaging locally:

cargo build --release --locked -p rustgis -p rustgis-cli
packaging/package.sh 0.1.0      # writes dist/

items.title: Open the app
items.text:
• In the browser: open web.rustgis.app. Nothing to install.
  • On the desktop: install RustGIS and start it. It opens the World Atlas sample: countries, cities, rivers and lakes from Natural Earth.
  • From source:
cargo run --release -p rustgis                  # opens the World Atlas sample
cargo run --release -p rustgis -- places.geojson
cargo run --release -p rustgis -- atlas.rgis   # a saved project
cargo run --release -p rustgis -- lesson.rgispkg   # a project package, opened unsaved

items.title: Five minutes with the World Atlas
items.text:
1. Explore. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom, and click a country to see its attributes in a pop-up. Press Home for the full extent, or pick a place from Home › Bookmarks.
  2. Style a layer. Click Countries in the Layers pane, then open the Style tab and Style › Symbology, choose Graduated Colors or Unique Values, and pick a colour scheme.
  3. Select. Home › Select By Attributes, enter continent = 'Asia', and press Apply. Open the attribute table with Ctrl+T. Rows and map features stay in sync.
  4. Analyse. Analyze › Buffer: choose Cities, 300 km, Dissolve: All, and Run. The result is added as a new layer, and the run is listed under Analyze › History.
  5. Change the view. View › Globe turns the map into a 3D globe; View › Projection offers Equal Earth, Robinson and other projections. Home › Add › Basemap switches the basemap or adds a web tile layer.
  6. Share. Publish › Export Map saves a PNG with labels and a scale bar. Home › New Layout makes a printable page with a legend and north arrow. Project › Save As writes a .rgis project.

Command search

Press Ctrl+K to find any command or geoprocessing tool by name.

items.title: Your own data
items.text: Home › Add Data (or drop files on the window) opens GeoJSON, CSV with longitude and latitude columns, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, GeoTIFFs and ASCII grids, and on the desktop also Shapefiles and GeoPackages. Project › New › Map starts from a blank map. See Data for the details of each format.

items.title: Ask the AI Assistant
items.text: Analyze › AI Assistant opens a chat pane. Choose a model provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, your ChatGPT account, Gemini, OpenRouter, a local Ollama, or any OpenAI-compatible server) and ask, for example, "Which 5 countries have the largest GDP?" or "Label the cities and zoom to Tokyo". See AI Assistant.

items.title: Choosing a language
items.text:
By default RustGIS follows your system's language (your browser's on the web) and falls back to English. To choose one yourself, open Settings › Language. The choice is remembered (in prefs.json beside the app's settings on the desktop, in the browser on the web). For one run, set RUSTGIS_LANGUAGE:

RUSTGIS_LANGUAGE=de cargo run --release -p rustgis

Only the interface is translated. Your data, layer and field names, command ids and the command line stay as they are, so scripts work in every language.

Chinese, Japanese and Korean need a CJK font. The desktop app uses one you have installed (Noto Sans CJK, Microsoft YaHei, Yu Gothic, Malgun Gothic, PingFang, Hiragino or Apple SD Gothic Neo); the web app downloads Noto Sans from assets.rustgis.app the first time you pick one of these languages. Map labels in images exported from the desktop app and the command line draw CJK text with the same installed font, whatever the interface language. Images exported from the web app have no CJK font yet, so CJK characters are left out of their labels.

items.title: Translating
items.text:
Each language is a catalog of English<TAB>Translation lines in crates/ui-egui/src/i18n/<code>.tsv. A missing entry shows in English, so translations can grow one line at a time, and corrections from native speakers are very welcome.

Every catalog uses the same keys. Pull requests can leave new strings out of the catalogs: the maintainer translates them before each release. To translate a new string, add a line with the exact English text, a tab, and the translation. Keep {placeholders} such as {n} or {name} (they may move), keep the line break (\n) in two-line ribbon labels, and leave product, format and key names (RustGIS, GeoJSON, CSV, Ctrl…) in English. The i18n tests check every catalog's format and placeholders:

cargo test -p rustgis-ui-egui i18n

Languages written right to left (Arabic, Persian, Hebrew) or needing complex shaping (Hindi, Thai) will follow once the UI toolkit supports them.

items.title: Install with an agent
items.text: Point your agent at the RustGIS skill and ask it to install RustGIS. The skill picks the platform, installs the app and rustgis-cli, checks the release checksum, and registers the MCP server. The same skill is how an agent manages the desktop app that is already open.

items.title: Microsoft Store
items.text: On Windows 10 and 11, the easiest way to install RustGIS is from the Microsoft Store, which signs the app and keeps it up to date:

items.title: Download
items.text:
Each GitHub release carries ready-to-run builds of the desktop app and rustgis-cli. The same files, grouped by platform, are mirrored at downloads.rustgis.app:

Platform File Windows x64 (installer, no admin rights) RustGIS-<version>-windows-x86_64-setup.exe Windows x64 (installer for all users) RustGIS-<version>-windows-x86_64.msi Windows x64 (no install) RustGIS-<version>-windows-x86_64-portable.zip (unzip and run rustgis.exe) Windows x64 (Microsoft Store package) RustGIS-<version>-windows-x86_64.msix macOS Apple Silicon RustGIS-<version>-macos-aarch64.dmg macOS Intel RustGIS-<version>-macos-x86_64.dmg Linux x64 / arm64 (Debian, Ubuntu) rustgis_<version>_amd64.deb / rustgis_<version>_arm64.deb Linux x64 / arm64 (Fedora, RHEL, openSUSE) rustgis-<version>-1.x86_64.rpm / rustgis-<version>-1.aarch64.rpm Linux x64 / arm64 (any distribution, no install) RustGIS-<version>-linux-x86_64.AppImage / RustGIS-<version>-linux-aarch64.AppImage Linux x64 / arm64 (other) RustGIS-<version>-linux-x86_64.tar.gz / RustGIS-<version>-linux-aarch64.tar.gz

On macOS the command line tool is a separate rustgis-cli-<version>-macos-<arch>.tar.gz; the other packages include it (the Windows installers and the MSIX add rustgis-cli to every new terminal). SHA256SUMS lists the checksum of every file.

On Windows, setup.exe installs for your account in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\RustGIS and needs no admin rights; the .msi installs for every user in Program Files and suits managed deployment (msiexec /i RustGIS-<version>-windows-x86_64.msi /qn). Both add a Start menu entry, open .rgis projects and uninstall from Settings › Apps.

The .msix is the package submitted to the Microsoft Store, which signs it. It is unsigned on the release page, so Windows only installs it from the Store; outside the Store, download an installer or the portable zip instead.

The macOS DMG and command line tool are signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so they open without a warning. From the release after 0.1.0, the notarization ticket is also stapled to RustGIS.app, so it opens even when the Mac cannot reach Apple's servers. If macOS says Apple could not verify RustGIS 0.1.0, connect to the internet and open it again, or run xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/RustGIS.app. The Windows builds are not yet signed: choose More info › Run anyway if SmartScreen warns about an unknown publisher.

items.title: Package managers
items.text:
RustGIS is also published to these package managers, which keep it up to date:

Platform Command Windows (winget) winget install OpenGeos.RustGIS macOS (Homebrew) brew install --cask opengeos/rustgis/rustgis macOS and Linux, command line tool only (Homebrew) brew install opengeos/rustgis/rustgis-cli Arch Linux (AUR) yay -S rustgis-bin (or any AUR helper) Fedora (COPR) sudo dnf copr enable giswqs/rustgis && sudo dnf install rustgis

winget installs for your account with the setup.exe; add --scope machine for the .msi. On Homebrew 5.1 and later, run brew trust opengeos/rustgis once before installing from the tap. Each package is the same build as the release page, and a new release reaches the package managers shortly after it is published (winget after Microsoft's review).

items.title: From source
items.text:
RustGIS builds from source with a recent stable Rust toolchain (1.90 or later).

git clone https://github.com/opengeos/RustGIS.git
cd RustGIS
cargo run --release -p rustgis            # the desktop app
cargo build --release -p rustgis-cli      # the command line tool

The build downloads the Natural Earth sample data (a few hundred KB) from rustgis-assets. To build offline, download the four files from https://assets.rustgis.app/data/ once and point the build at them:

RUSTGIS_DATA_DIR=/path/to/data cargo build --release

items.title: Web app
items.text:
RustGIS also runs in the browser, compiled to WebAssembly: open web.rustgis.app. It is the same app with three differences:

  • Open and Add Data use the browser's file picker, and you can drop files on the page. GeoJSON, CSV, GeoTIFF, ASCII grids and .rgis projects work; Shapefiles need the desktop app.
  • Save and Export download the file. Save As, and the first Save of a project, ask for the file name first; the browser decides which folder downloads go to (Firefox, for one, saves to its Downloads folder unless told to ask). A project opened from a file is named after it, and Save downloads it under that name again.
  • The interface uses the built-in font, because a web page can't read installed fonts.

The web app opens the way Settings › Start-up says (remembered in the browser). The URL can override that for one visit: add ?blank to start with an empty project, ?projection=EPSG:3010 (a supported projected EPSG code, a preset id such as robinson, or globe) to start in another projection, ?extent=10.5,55,24.5,69.5 (west, south, east, north in degrees) to open on an area, ?lang=de (or any language code) to pick the interface language, or ?webgl to force WebGL2. Combine them with &, so a self-hosted build can link to ?blank&projection=EPSG:3010&extent=10.5,55,24.5,69.5.

Links can carry data too: ?data=<address> adds a file by its web address (any format Add Data reads, downloaded in the background; repeat it for up to 16, and the map zooms to the first that lands with something to show), ?style=<address> adds a MapLibre style, ?tiles=<template> a tile layer, and ?zarr=<address> opens Add Zarr Variable on a Zarr store. Percent-encode an address holding &, # or spaces (encodeURIComponent); a + stays a +. The server must allow the browser to fetch the file (CORS); a file that can't be added is said in a notice. For example, ?blank&data=https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/feed/v1.0/summary/2.5_week.geojson opens the past week's earthquakes.

?project=<address> opens a whole project by its web address: a .rgis file (or a .rgispkg package), or any address that answers with a project's JSON, such as an API that builds the project on the fly. Its maps, layers, symbology and view open as saved, so one link shares a styled map. The project replaces the start-up one, so ?data=, ?stac=, ?style=, ?tiles= and ?zarr= are left out beside it (a notice says so). The data the project points to is read as it would be from a saved file, and its servers must allow the browser to fetch it (CORS), as must the project's.

?stac=<address> opens STAC Search on a STAC item or collection: an item's footprint is drawn and its default asset (its true-colour visual image, else its first GeoTIFF) added, signed first when it is a Microsoft Planetary Computer one; a collection is chosen in the dialog, with its API, ready to search. For example, ?stac=https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1/collections/sentinel-2-l2a/items/S2B_MSIL2A_20240727T102559_R108_T32TLS_20240727T131405 opens a Sentinel-2 scene of Lake Geneva.

?embed runs the app inside another page, as the Python package's notebook widget does: it starts blank, keeps its settings in memory rather than in the browser, and exchanges the project with the page that frames it through postMessage (the messages are described in apps/rustgis-web/src/embed.rs).

items.title: Install the web app
items.text:
The web app installs like an app on phones, tablets and computers, with its own icon and a window without the browser's toolbars, and starts without a network connection once it has been opened online. Nothing is downloaded from an app store, and it updates itself from web.rustgis.app.

Platform How iPhone and iPad Open web.rustgis.app in Safari, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen Android Open it in Chrome, tap the ⋮ menu, then Install app (or Add to Home screen) Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS In Chrome or Edge, click the install icon at the right of the address bar (or ⋮ › Cast, save and share › Install page as app) Mac (Safari 17 or later) File › Add to Dock

To remove it, delete it like any other app: long-press the icon on a phone or tablet, or use Uninstall in the app window's menu on a computer.

Offline, the installed app opens the World Atlas sample and the files you open, but not basemap tiles, web data, plugins or the AI Assistant, which need the network. When a new version has been published while the app is open, a notice offers to reload into it; otherwise the next launch picks it up. Two things to know on iPhone and iPad: iOS gives a web page less memory than a desktop browser, so very large rasters may not open, and it can clear the offline copy when the device runs short of storage, so the next launch then needs a connection.

To build it yourself, install Trunk, the wasm32-unknown-unknown target and clang (it compiles the Zstandard decoder used for GeoTIFFs to WebAssembly). Linux distributions' clang can; on macOS, Apple's can't, so install llvm with Homebrew and put its bin first on your PATH. Then:

cd apps/rustgis-web
trunk serve          # http://127.0.0.1:8772
trunk build --release   # output in dist/web
cargo xtask web-pwa ../../dist/web   # add the service worker (offline start), as the deploy does

The service worker is left out of trunk serve, so a development build is never served from a stale cache.

items.title: Fonts
items.text: RustGIS uses an installed sans-serif when it finds one (Segoe UI, San Francisco, Inter, Noto Sans, Open Sans or DejaVu Sans) and falls back to a built-in face. Set RUSTGIS_BUILTIN_FONTS=1 to always use the built-in face.

items.title: If RustGIS closes unexpectedly
items.text:
The desktop app writes its internal errors to crash.log in its settings folder: one that closed the app, and also one it recovered from (an error in the AI Assistant, for example, stops the request and says so in the chat instead of closing the app). The folder is %APPDATA%\RustGIS on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support/RustGIS on macOS, and $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/rustgis on Linux (~/.config/rustgis when that isn't set). The next launch moves the log to crash-last.log and names the file in a notice.

Attach it to a bug report. It holds the version, the operating system, the error message and where in RustGIS it happened. An error message can quote what RustGIS was working on, such as a file path or a layer name, so read the log first and remove anything you don't want to share.

items.title: MCP Server
items.text:
rustgis-cli mcp runs RustGIS as a Model Context Protocol server, so an AI agent such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code or Codex can make maps with it. The agent opens data, runs any RustGIS command or geoprocessing tool, reads attribute tables, looks at the map as an image and looks things up in this documentation.

rustgis-cli mcp --sample                # the World Atlas sample
rustgis-cli mcp --data parcels.geojson  # your own data (--data more than once, or --project p.rgis)
rustgis-cli mcp --yes                   # also allow file and network access
rustgis-cli mcp --attach [--yes]        # the desktop app that is already open (its MCP Relay)

The server talks over standard input and output, so you don't start it yourself: you tell your agent how to start it (below), and the agent runs it. Each agent gets its own project, held in memory until the agent saves it.

items.title: Adding it to an agent
items.text:
Claude Code:

claude mcp add rustgis -- rustgis-cli mcp --sample

Codex:

codex mcp add rustgis -- rustgis-cli mcp --sample

Claude Desktop (claude_desktop_config.json), Cursor (~/.cursor/mcp.json) and other clients that use an mcpServers list:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "rustgis": {
      "command": "rustgis-cli",
      "args": ["mcp", "--sample"]
    }
  }
}

VS Code (.vscode/mcp.json):

{
  "servers": {
    "rustgis": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "rustgis-cli",
      "args": ["mcp", "--sample"]
    }
  }
}

If the agent can't find rustgis-cli, give its full path (see Installation). Then ask, for example:

  • "Which 5 countries have the largest GDP? Show them on the map."
  • "Buffer the cities by 200 km, colour the result by population and show me the map."
  • "Load ~/data/parcels.geojson, label the parcels with their owner and export the map to parcels.png." (this reads and writes files, so it needs --yes)

items.title: Managing the open desktop app
items.text:
By default each agent gets its own project in memory. To drive the project that is open in the desktop app instead, tick Let your Agents Control RustGIS in the AI Assistant's settings. It starts the relay and shows what an agent needs to connect: the MCP server configuration, and the claude mcp add / codex mcp add commands. While it's ticked, attached agents may also read and write files and use the network, without --yes. RustGIS remembers the choice and starts the relay with the app. The MCP Relay command (Help menu, or Command Search with Ctrl+K) starts the relay too, without that: attached agents then have the access their --yes asks for. The relay is off until the box is ticked or that command runs. While it runs, the status bar shows MCP relay · n attached, where n is the number of authenticated clients; hovering shows Stop MCP relay, and clicking it stops the relay.

rustgis-cli mcp --attach                 # the open app on 127.0.0.1:8767
rustgis-cli mcp --attach 9000 --yes      # another port, with file and network access

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "rustgis-app": {
      "command": "rustgis-cli",
      "args": ["mcp", "--attach", "--yes"]
    }
  }
}

Attached calls run on the open app's session through the same tools and refusal policy as the private server. File and network commands need --yes, unless Let your Agents Control RustGIS is ticked.

An agent the app starts itself gets a run-scoped token instead of the relay's own: rustgis-cli mcp --attach PORT --token-file FILE. Each such grant carries its own file and network permission, and the app revokes it when it's done with the agent; that closes its connections and removes its file.

items.title: Relay requirements
items.text:
• Off until asked. Only ui.mcpRelay starts a listener: run directly, or by ticking Let your Agents Control RustGIS (also at launch, when it was left ticked). ui.mcpRelay with no parameters or with the same port reports the address it already listens on. A different explicit port is refused until the relay is stopped. ui.mcpRelay {"stop": true} stops it and is idempotent. The default port is 8767.
  • Loopback only. Relay::bind refuses any non-loopback address before a socket is opened; the app's ui.mcpRelay binds 127.0.0.1.
  • Private token. Each run draws 16 bytes from the operating system's random source, written as 32 hex characters. The token file is {port}.token in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/rustgis when that is an absolute folder, otherwise in a per-user folder under the system temporary folder. The folder must be owned by the current user and not accessible to others. The file must be a regular file owned by the current user, without group or other access. A file that is a symlink is refused. rustgis-cli mcp --attach reads it with read_token(port). The token never appears on a command line. The file is removed when the relay stops.
  • App-granted access. Relay::set_allow_access(true) lets connections attached with the relay's own token use files and the network whether or not they asked; the desktop app sets it while Let your Agents Control RustGIS is ticked. This includes any process running as the same user that can read that token, not just agents launched by RustGIS. It is checked for every call. Turning the setting off stops the relay and disconnects its clients, including a relay started manually. A failed launch clears the saved setting and reports the error in the app.
  • Grants. Relay::grant(access) writes a run-scoped token to {port}-{run}-{n}.token in the same private folder (run is random per relay run). A grant asked for after the relay stopped is refused. A connection that attaches with it gets the grant's permission. Dropping the grant removes the file, forgets the token and closes its connections. Stopping the relay removes every grant's file.
  • Attach first. A connection's first non-empty line must be a rustgis/attach message carrying the token. It must arrive within 5 seconds, measured from connection, and be at most 4096 bytes including its newline. The token is compared without early exit. A connection that fails this is closed. The access flag sets what that connection may do; the per-call refusal policy still applies. A repeat attach may change access.
  • Handshake and idle limits. Attached clients that send nothing for 300 seconds are closed. A reply write that takes longer than 10 seconds closes the connection.
  • Connection caps. At most 16 open connections, and at most 4 that have not attached. A connection beyond either cap is dropped without a reply.
  • Queue cap. At most 64 messages wait for the app's frame. A request beyond that gets error -32001 (the app is busy; try again) if it expects a reply.
  • Bounded request waits. A request waits up to 60 seconds for the app to run it. If it is still pending then, it is cancelled and never runs; the client gets error -32002. If it is already running, the client waits one more 60-second interval. If the reply still has not come, the client gets error -32003 (its outcome is unknown), and the command may still complete later.
  • Stop. Stopping the relay, or dropping its last owner, closes the listener and every client, drops queued messages unrun, and removes the token file. A waiting request ends at once, checked every 25 milliseconds.
  • Wake. A queued message or a change in the attached-client count wakes the UI thread so it draws a frame. A relay started before the first frame installs its wake on the first logic call after that frame exists.
  • Shared framing. Each message is one JSON-RPC message per line. After attach, messages and replies are read with read_message_max at 64 MiB (MAX_LINE), the limit counting the newline. The attach line is read at most 4096 bytes including its newline (see Attach first). After an oversized line on a socket the relay sends a -32700 error and closes that connection. On standard input the reader skips the rest of the line and continues. IO errors name neither standard input nor a socket.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
These behavioral tests in crates/assistant/src/relay.rs check the requirements above:

  • Loopback bind and command run: relay_runs_a_command_on_the_target_session
  • Token required: relay_drops_connections_without_the_token
  • Parse error after attach: relay_returns_parse_error_after_attach_and_stays_usable
  • File commands need --yes: relay_refuses_file_commands_without_yes
  • Timed-out command never runs: relay_cancels_a_timed_out_command_so_it_never_runs
  • Stop cleanup: relay_stop_closes_clients_and_removes_the_token
  • Last owner drop: relay_last_owner_drop_closes_the_listener
  • Unauthenticated cap: relay_caps_unauthenticated_connections
  • Oversized pre-attach line: relay_refuses_an_oversized_unauthenticated_line
  • Token random and private: relay_token_is_random_and_private
  • Client count and wake: relay_counts_authenticated_clients_and_wakes_on_change
  • Stop ends a reply wait: relay_stop_ends_a_reply_wait_and_the_command_never_runs
  • Running command reported as unknown: relay_reports_a_running_command_past_its_wait_as_unknown
  • Handshake deadline: relay_closes_a_trickling_handshake_at_its_deadline
  • App-granted access: relay_app_lets_agents_use_files_without_yes
  • Grants are scoped and revocable: relay_grants_are_scoped_and_revocable

items.title: Tools
items.text:
Tool What it does list_layers The map: its layers (name, type, feature count, fields, visibility, selection), its web tile layers (XYZ, WMS, vector tiles), basemap, centre and scale view_map The map as a PNG image, at the current view search_commands Finds RustGIS commands by words: their ids, ribbon locations and parameters run_command Runs a command by id with JSON parameters; each run is one undo step. The result names the layers it added (layersAdded) and what the command said beside it (notices), including any parameters it ignored (layer.moveDown ignores 'steps' (it reads layer)) search_tools Finds geoprocessing tools by words describe_tool A geoprocessing tool's parameters run_tool Runs a geoprocessing tool; its output is added to the map as a new layer (with layersAdded and notices as for run_command) read_features A layer's attribute rows, optionally only those matching a where clause, sorted search_docs Searches this documentation and returns the best matching sections read_doc Reads a documentation page or section as Markdown; offset (1-based line) and limit (default 2000 lines) page through long results using next_offset

These are the AI Assistant's tools, plus view_map. Every page of this documentation is also a resource (rustgis://docs/cli.md, rustgis://docs/user-guide/maps.md…) that a client can attach to a conversation.

items.title: What the agent may do
items.text:
Your agent asks you before each tool call, and the server adds its own limits:

  • Commands that read or write files, connect to an address on the internet or run a plugin's command run only when the server was started with --yes, as does opening a project from text (it could bring in web layers). Without it, the agent can still work with the data you gave the server and with the built-in sample, basemaps and geoprocessing. view_map draws the web tile layers the project you opened already has, fetching their tiles.
  • Plugin management, scripts, tasks, models and the GeoLibre runner are never run from here.
  • In private-server mode, opening, replacing and undoing in the project are allowed: the project is the agent's own. With --attach, these operations affect the project open in the desktop app.

Installed plugins load first, as with the other subcommands (--no-plugins skips them). Notes such as "MCP server ready" go to standard error; standard output carries only the protocol.

items.title: Local-agent approvals
items.text:
Local agents launched by the assistant use Relay::grant_reviewed(auto), not an unrestricted run grant. With automatic approval off, gated tool calls wait in a RustGIS-side queue scoped to that grant and exact message, including all tool calls in a batch. --yes and the general relay checkbox do not bypass it. An approval cannot revive an expired request; revoking the grant or stopping the relay cancels pending work. Explicit automatic approval bypasses this extra queue for that run. Ordinary MCP clients retain the access policy described above.

Stopping the relay through its command or status-bar control also turns off its remembered agent-control choice. Copyable setup commands are labelled for POSIX shells or PowerShell and quote the executable path literally; use the matching shell.

items.title: Plugins
items.text:
Plugins add commands and geoprocessing tools to RustGIS. A plugin is a WebAssembly module with a plugin.json manifest, packaged as a .rgplugin file. The same file runs in the desktop app, on the command line and in the web app.

Browse the registry at plugins.rustgis.app. Plugin sources, the SDK and the registry live in opengeos/rustgis-plugins.

items.title: Using plugins
items.text:
Open Plugins › Plugin Manager:

  • Browse lists the plugins in the registry. Install downloads the plugin, checks it against the SHA-256 the registry published, and shows what the plugin may do before it loads.
  • Installed lists your plugins: turn them on or off, update them, or uninstall them.
  • Settings installs a .rgplugin file. You can also drop the file on the window. It also sets the registry address (empty means the RustGIS registry). On the desktop, it can load a plugin from its folder while you develop it.

A plugin's commands and tools appear on the Plugins tab, in a group named after the plugin, or on the plugin's own tab if it has one. Its commands are also in command search, and its tools are in the Tools pane under Plugins ›.

The desktop app keeps installed packages in its data folder (plugins/ beside the GeoLibre runner, or $RUSTGIS_PLUGINS_DIR) and loads them at startup. The web app remembers the plugins you installed from the registry and downloads them again on your next visit. Packages installed from files are kept too, if they are small enough for the browser's storage.

On the command line:

rustgis-cli plugins                          # installed plugins
rustgis-cli plugins browse                   # the registry
rustgis-cli plugins get vector-toolkit       # install from the registry
rustgis-cli plugins install my.rgplugin      # install a file (or a plugin folder)
rustgis-cli plugins disable vector-toolkit   # enable / disable / uninstall <id>

rustgis-cli run --sample \
  --cmd 'gp.run={"tool":"plugin:vector-toolkit/hexagon-grid","params":{"input":"Countries","size":300}}' \
  --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"hex.png"}'
rustgis-cli run --plugin ./dev-plugin/ --sample --cmd 'plugin:my-plugin/hello'   # load for one run

items.title: Safety
items.text:
Plugins run in a sandbox: an interpreter (wasmi) with no access to files, the network, the clock or anything else outside the module. A plugin reaches RustGIS only through the requests described below, and RustGIS checks each one:

  • Every plugin can read the map: its layers, their features and the view.
  • With the edit permission, it can change the project. It can run commands that edit it and add layers. A plugin command that changes the project is one undo step, and it is rolled back if the command fails.
  • With the files permission, it can run commands that read or write files the user names, and its tools can take a file the user picks (a file parameter).
  • With the network permission (and edit), it can add web tile layers (map.addTiles). The map then loads tiles from the addresses the plugin gave, and an address can carry what the plugin read from the project, so this is a permission of its own. A command that would bring in a tile layer some other way (importing a map file) has it taken out again without network.
  • No plugin may run the user's scripts, tasks or models, install or locate other software, manage plugins, replace the project, or step through undo history.

A process plugin is the exception: it is a program on your computer, not sandboxed, and the install prompt says so.

The install prompt lists these permissions. Each call has a fuel budget, so a plugin stuck in a loop is stopped. Memory is capped at 512 MB, and requests and replies are size-limited. A plugin that traps, panics or returns garbage produces an error message, never a crash.

The registry is curated: plugins are reviewed before they are listed, and packages are hash-pinned. A blocklist.json beside the registry withdraws a plugin (every version, or one package) from every install. RustGIS checks it when you browse the registry and at startup.

items.title: Writing a plugin
items.text:
Start from plugins/hello in the plugins repository. It uses the rustgis-plugin SDK crate:

use rustgis_plugin::{Kind, Request, ToolOutput, Value, geojson, host, json};

fn handle(req: Request) -> Result<Value, String> {
    match (req.kind, req.id.as_str()) {
        (Kind::Command, "layer-report") => {
            let n = host::layers()?.as_array().map_or(0, Vec::len);
            host::notify(&format!("{n} layers"));
            Ok(json!({"layers": n}))
        }
        (Kind::Tool, "bounding-boxes") => {
            let boxes: Vec<Value> = req.features("input")?.iter().filter_map(|f| {
                let b = geojson::bbox(&geojson::positions(&f["geometry"]))?;
                Some(geojson::feature(geojson::polygon(&[[b[0], b[1]], [b[2], b[1]], [b[2], b[3]], [b[0], b[3]]]), json!({})))
            }).collect();
            Ok(ToolOutput::new().layer("Boxes", geojson::collection(boxes)).into())
        }
        (_, other) => Err(format!("unknown '{other}'")),
    }
}

rustgis_plugin::export!(handle);

cargo build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown

items.title: plugin.json
items.text:
{
  "id": "hello-rustgis",
  "name": "Hello RustGIS",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "What it does, in a sentence or two.",
  "author": "You",
  "homepage": "https://github.com/you/your-plugin",
  "license": "MIT",
  "entry": "plugin.wasm",
  "abi": 1,
  "minRustgisVersion": "0.1.0",
  "permissions": ["edit"],
  "commands": [
    { "id": "layer-report", "label": "Layer\nReport", "help": "Shown on hover.", "icon": "stats", "params": "{}" }
  ],
  "tools": [
    {
      "id": "bounding-boxes", "name": "Bounding Boxes", "summary": "One line.", "toolbox": "Hello",
      "params": [
        { "name": "input", "label": "Input features", "kind": "vectorLayer", "required": true },
        { "name": "whole", "label": "One box for the whole layer", "kind": "bool", "default": false }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "i18n": { "de": { "Layer\nReport": "Ebenen-\nbericht" } }
}
  • id: lower-case letters, digits and hyphens. Commands and tools get ids plugin:<id>/<command>, which the ribbon, command search, scripts and rustgis-cli use.
  • version and minRustgisVersion look like 1.2.3. RustGIS refuses a plugin that needs a newer RustGIS.
  • permissions: edit, files and network (see Safety). Ask only for what you use.
  • commands[].icon: the name of one of RustGIS's own icons (stats, zoom_full, bookmark, buffer…), or a puzzle piece when it isn't one.
  • Tool parameter kinds: layer, vectorLayer, polygonLayer, pointLayer, field, numericField, number, text, choice (with choices), bool and file (see File parameters).
  • i18n translates the plugin's own text into the interface language, by language code (de, zh-CN…). See Translations.
  • skills (optional) lists skills for the AI Assistant that the package carries. See Skills.

A package is a zip archive named <id>-<version>.rgplugin. It holds plugin.json and the module at its root, or inside one top-level folder. Packages are at most 64 MB, and modules at most 48 MB.

items.title: File parameters
items.text:
A tool can read a file the user picks, such as a NetCDF model run, with a file parameter. The plugin needs the files permission:

{ "name": "model", "label": "Model output", "kind": "file", "required": true, "extensions": ["nc", "nc4"] }
  • The Tools pane shows a path box with a Browse button. extensions (without the dot; up to 16) filters the file picker; leave it out for any file.
  • On the desktop and the command line the value is a path, and RustGIS reads the file. In the web app, which has no paths, the user picks the file and its contents go with the run. A script can do the same with {"name": "run.nc", "data": base64}.
  • The tool gets the file in the request's files, by parameter name, as {"name": "run.nc", "data": base64}. The parameter itself holds just the file name.
  • Files are at most 64 MB. The Geoprocessing history keeps the file's name, not its contents.
  • RustGIS versions before file parameters refuse a plugin that has one, so set minRustgisVersion to the first version with them.

items.title: Translations
items.text:
A plugin speaks the interface language through its i18n table: for each language code, its English strings and their translations, written exactly as they appear in plugin.json (\n included):

"i18n": {
  "de": { "Bounding Boxes": "Begrenzungsrahmen", "Input features": "Eingabe-Features" },
  "zh-CN": { "Bounding Boxes": "边界框", "Input features": "输入要素" }
}
  • It covers the plugin's name and description, command labels and help, tool names, summaries and toolboxes, parameter labels and choice values, and the tab, group and menu labels. A string with no translation shows in English.
  • RustGIS's interface languages are de, es, fr, it, nl, pt, ru, tr, az, id, vi, zh, ja and ko. A code with a region matches its language: zh-CN serves zh.
  • The registry copies the name and description translations into registry.json, so the Plugin Manager lists plugins in the interface language before they are installed.
  • Messages a plugin builds while it runs can follow the interface language too: every request carries its code as lang. In the SDK that is req.lang, and req.tr looks a message up in i18n.
  • Up to 64 languages and 20,000 translated strings in all.

items.title: A tab of its own
items.text:
By default a plugin's commands and tools get a group on the Plugins tab. A plugin can have a ribbon tab of its own instead. The tab sits at the end of the tab strip, and Help › Ribbon can hide it like any other. Declare it in plugin.json:

"tab": {
  "label": "Explorer",
  "groups": [
    {
      "label": "Go To",
      "items": [
        { "menu": "Continent", "icon": "zoom_world", "help": "Go to a continent.", "items": ["go-africa", "go-europe"] },
        "random-place"
      ]
    },
    { "label": "Inspect", "items": ["layer-report", "tool:field-summary"] }
  ]
}
  • items lists the buttons. An item is a command id, tool:<id> (which opens that tool in the Tools pane), or a dropdown menu whose items are command ids or tool:<id>.
  • A tab has 1 to 8 groups, a group has 1 to 16 items, and a menu has 1 to 32 entries. Every entry must name one of the plugin's own commands or tools.
  • The label can't be the name of one of RustGIS's tabs (Map, Insert, Analysis, Plugins…). The i18n translations apply to the tab, group and menu labels too.

Map Explorer is an example.

items.title: What a plugin can ask for
items.text:
Inside a request, host::call(op, params) sends one of these to RustGIS:

Request Answer host.info RustGIS's version, the ABI, the plugin's id and permissions host.layers [{id, name, raster, visible, geometry, features, selected, active, fields: [{name, type}]}] host.features {layer, selected?, limit?} the layer's features as GeoJSON; each feature has its row host.view {center: [lon, lat], scale, projection} host.notify {text, error?} shows a message in the status bar host.addLayer {name, geojson} adds a layer (edit) map.addTiles {url, kind?, name?, attribution?, maxZoom?, overlay?, replace?} adds a web tile layer (edit and network) any command id (layer.zoomTo, select.byAttributes, layer.symbology…) what the command returns, within the plugin's permissions

In the web app a command can't wait for a download, so where layer.addUrl has to download a file whole it answers {"pending": true, "url": …} there: RustGIS downloads the data off the frame and adds the layer when it lands, as Home › Add Data › From URL does. A PMTiles archive, a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF or a FlatGeobuf or GeoParquet read in place is added at once, as elsewhere.

rustgis-cli commands lists every command id and its parameters.

Tools work differently. A tool receives its layer parameters' features as GeoJSON (only the selected features when a layer has a selection), and its file parameters' files. It returns new layers, standalone tables or a selection, plus messages for the Geoprocessing history. RustGIS adds the results as it does for built-in tools, with undo. Tools can log, but they make no host requests.

In the desktop app a plugin tool runs in the background, so the map and the rest of the window stay usable: the Tools pane shows the line the tool last logged, or a process plugin's last progress message, and a Cancel button. Cancel stops a process plugin's program; a WebAssembly tool runs on to its end and its result is dropped. One plugin tool runs at a time. gp.run, scripts and rustgis-cli still wait for the result.

items.title: The ABI (version 1)
items.text:
The SDK implements this; it is described here for other languages.

The module is wasm32 with no imports except these three, in module rustgis:

  • call(ptr: i32, len: i32) -> i32 runs the host request at ptr ({"op": "...", "params": {...}}). It returns the length of the reply, which is {"ok": value} or {"error": "text"}, or -1 when there is none.
  • result(ptr: i32) copies that reply to ptr. Allocate the length call returned first.
  • log(ptr: i32, len: i32) logs a UTF-8 line.

The module exports:

  • memory.
  • rustgis_alloc(len: i32) -> i32, which returns room for len bytes. RustGIS writes the request there.
  • rustgis_call(ptr: i32, len: i32) -> i64, which handles the request and returns reply_ptr << 32 | reply_len. The reply is {"ok": value} or {"error": "text"}.

Requests are {"abi": 1, "kind": "command" | "tool", "id": "...", "params": {...}, "layers": {...}, "lang": "de"}. lang is the interface language's code (en for English). Tools also get layers, which maps each layer's name to its FeatureCollection, and, when they have file parameters, files, which maps each one's name to {"name", "data"} with the file's contents in base64. A tool's ok value is {"layers": [{"name", "geojson"}], "tables": [...], "selection": {"layer", "rows"}, "messages": [...]}.

Each call gets a fresh instance, so a module keeps no state between calls and need not free memory. The fuel budget is about 2×10⁹ instructions for a command and 4×10¹⁰ for a tool.

items.title: Process plugins
items.text:
A process plugin is a program on your computer instead of a WebAssembly module: a Python script, or an executable in any language. It can use the file system, threads and any library, which lets existing analysis code (numpy, xarray, GDAL…) become a plugin without a rewrite. It is not sandboxed: it can do anything you can. The install prompt says so, and the Plugin Manager marks it Not sandboxed. Process plugins run on the desktop and the command line, not in the web app.

{
  "id": "hello-python",
  "name": "Hello Python",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "runtime": "process",
  "run": { "windows": ["python", "main.py"], "default": ["python3", "main.py"] },
  "permissions": [],
  "commands": [{ "id": "layer-count", "label": "Count\nLayers" }],
  "tools": [{
    "id": "feature-count", "name": "Count Features", "summary": "Counts a layer's features.",
    "params": [{ "name": "input", "label": "Input layer", "kind": "vectorLayer", "required": true }]
  }]
}
  • "runtime": "process" and run: the program and its arguments, started in the plugin's folder. A bare name (python3) is looked up on PATH; a relative path (bin/tool) is in the plugin's folder. run can name a program per platform (windows, macos, linux, and default for the rest). There is no entry.
  • Commands, tools, tabs, translations and permissions work as for WebAssembly plugins. Permissions still decide which host requests RustGIS answers, but they don't limit what the program itself can do.
  • A .rgplugin holds the plugin's files (the manifest, scripts, executables). Installing it unpacks them to unpacked/<id>/ in the plugins folder, keeping executables executable. A plugin folder installed for development (Plugin Manager › Settings, or rustgis-cli plugins install ./folder) runs where it is.

items.title: The protocol
items.text:
Each command or tool call starts the program once. It speaks the ABI's requests and replies over its standard input and output, one JSON object per line:

  1. RustGIS writes the request: {"abi", "kind", "id", "params", "layers", "files", "lang"}, as a WebAssembly module gets it.
  2. The program writes lines:
  3. {"call": {"op": "...", "params": {...}}}: a host request. RustGIS answers with one line, {"ok": value} or {"error": "text"}.
  4. {"log": "text"}: a line for the log (and a tool's run messages).
  5. {"progress": "text"}: what a tool is doing now, shown while it runs and not kept in its messages: a line per step of a long run, say.
  6. Last, {"ok": value} or {"error": "text"}: the result.
  7. RustGIS then closes the program's input; a program still running a few seconds later is stopped.

Output lines that aren't protocol messages are logged and skipped, since libraries print (even JSON), and so is the program's error output. A command is stopped after 2 minutes; a tool runs until it finishes or is cancelled (the desktop app runs it in the background: see What a plugin can ask for).

The plugin above, in Python with no SDK:

import json
import sys


def call(op, params):
    """Sends a request to RustGIS and returns its answer."""
    print(json.dumps({"call": {"op": op, "params": params}}), flush=True)
    reply = json.loads(sys.stdin.readline())
    if "error" in reply:
        raise RuntimeError(reply["error"])
    return reply["ok"]


req = json.loads(sys.stdin.readline())
try:
    if req["id"] == "layer-count":
        n = len(call("host.layers", {}))
        call("host.notify", {"text": f"The map has {n} layers."})
        result = {"ok": {"layers": n}}
    elif req["id"] == "feature-count":
        layer = req["params"]["input"]
        n = len(req["layers"][layer]["features"])
        result = {"ok": {"layers": [], "messages": [f"{layer} has {n} features."]}}
    else:
        result = {"error": f"unknown command '{req['id']}'"}
except Exception as e:
    result = {"error": str(e)}
print(json.dumps(result), flush=True)

items.title: Python environments
items.text:
A Python plugin can have RustGIS make its environment, so its users don't install Python or any package themselves:

"runtime": "process",
"python": { "version": "3.12", "requirements": "requirements.txt" },
"run": ["python", "main.py"]
  • python in run is then that environment's interpreter, on every platform.
  • RustGIS makes the environment when the plugin is installed: in the background in the desktop app (the Plugin Manager shows how it's going, and a Prepare button makes it again), and before the command returns in rustgis-cli plugins install and get. rustgis-cli plugins prepare <id> and the plugin.prepare command make it on demand.
  • It uses uv, which RustGIS downloads once (a pinned version, checked against its pinned SHA-256; RUSTGIS_UV names one to use instead, which is then trusted as it is, unchecked). uv installs a standalone Python of the version asked for and the packages in the requirements file, from PyPI. Pythons and uv's cache are shared in tools/ in the plugins folder; each plugin's environment is in envs/<id>/. One environment is made at a time per plugin, even across the app and rustgis-cli.
  • The environment is made again when the Python version or the requirements change (a plugin update), and removed with the plugin. Until it's ready, the plugin's calls fail with a message saying how to prepare it.
  • The first install downloads Python and the packages: tens to hundreds of MB, depending on them. The install prompt says so.

items.title: Skills
items.text:
A plugin can carry skills for the AI Assistant: instructions for a kind of task, which the assistant reads when a request needs them. Put each in skills/<name>/SKILL.md in the package and list the names in plugin.json:

"skills": ["flood-map"]

A SKILL.md starts with front matter giving the same name and a description that says when to use it, then the instructions in Markdown (the Agent Skills format). The assistant knows it as <plugin id>:<name> (hello-rustgis:flood-map) while the plugin is enabled. A SKILL.md is at most 64 KB, and a plugin has at most 32 skills.

A package of skills alone, with no code, says "runtime": "skills". It has no module, commands, tools, tab or permissions. Nothing in it runs, and it installs and works like any other plugin, in the desktop app, on the command line and in the web app:

{
  "id": "flood-skills",
  "name": "Flood mapping skills",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "runtime": "skills",
  "skills": ["flood-map", "gauge-report"]
}

items.title: Publishing a plugin
items.text:
Open a pull request on opengeos/rustgis-plugins that adds registry/<id>.json:

  • For a plugin whose source is in that repository: {"id": "...", "path": "plugins/<dir>", "categories": [...]}.
  • For one you publish elsewhere: {"id": "...", "source": {"url": "https://…/<id>-<version>.rgplugin", "sha256": "…"}, "categories": [...]}.

CI builds or downloads the package and checks its manifest and module. A maintainer then reviews it. Once merged, it is published at plugins.rustgis.app with its hash.

items.title: Privacy
items.text: The RustGIS desktop app and command line collect no analytics, telemetry or usage data. Your geospatial data and projects stay on your device unless you choose to share or export them.

items.title: Online services
items.text: Some features ask a public server for an answer, and send it what the answer needs: Find Place and the search box send the place you look up to OpenStreetMap's Nominatim, and Directions sends a route's start, stops and destination to the Valhalla server run by FOSSGIS (it asks you first). Web basemaps and data added from a web address are fetched from their servers. Nothing else about you or your data is sent with them.

items.title: Website analytics
items.text:
The websites we host, the documentation at rustgis.app and the web app at web.rustgis.app, use Google Analytics 4 to count page visits and see which pages are used. Google receives your IP address, the page you are on, the referring page and general device and browser information, and sets its own cookies in your browser. It is governed by Google's privacy policy.

Analytics never see the data you work with: layers, files, projects and coordinates are processed in your browser and are not sent to Google. The web app reports its address trimmed to the site and path (https://web.rustgis.app/), without the query string. The documentation reports the full page address, which names the page you are reading and, after a search, the words you searched for.

You can block analytics with a content blocker or your browser's tracking protection; the sites work normally without them. Analytics run only on the sites we host: the measurement ID is added when those sites are deployed, so the desktop app, the command line and any copy you build yourself never load them.

items.title: Python
items.text:
The rustgis package runs the RustGIS engine inside Python, headless. It opens data and projects, runs any command and geoprocessing tool, styles layers, renders maps and saves projects that the desktop app opens as they are. There is no app to install and no server to run: the engine is a native module built for Windows, macOS and Linux, for Python 3.12 and later.

pip install rustgis               # pip install "rustgis[geopandas]" for GeoDataFrames

A getting-started notebook walks through what follows; open it in Colab to try it without installing anything.

items.title: A first session
items.text:
import rustgis

s = rustgis.Session(sample=True)                    # the World Atlas sample
s.layers()                                          # id, name, type, features, fields…
s.run("gp.run", tool="buffer", params={"input": "Cities", "distance": 100})
s.run("layer.symbology", layer="Countries", type="graduated", field="pop_est")
s.to_png("map.png", width=1600, height=900)
s.save("atlas.rgis")

In Jupyter, a session on the last line of a cell shows its map as a picture. For the app itself, use a Map.

items.title: The app in a notebook
items.text:
rustgis.Map shows the RustGIS app (ribbon, panes, map) in the cell, kept in step with its session: what Python adds or styles appears in the app, and what you do in the app (an edit, a new layer, a pan) is back in the session for Python to read. It needs anywidget, and works in JupyterLab, Notebook, VS Code and Colab.

pip install "rustgis[jupyter]"

m = rustgis.Map(sample=True)                         # height="800px" by default
m                                                   # the app, in the cell

m.add_geojson("sites.geojson", name="Sites")        # appears in the app
m.run("layer.symbology", layer="Sites", type="unique", field="name")
m.set_center(10, 50, scale=5_000_000)
m.add_tiles("https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png", name="OpenStreetMap")

m.info()["center"]                                  # where the app's map is now
m.save("sites.rgis")                                # with what was done in the app
m.run_in_app("ui.language", code="de")              # a command only the app has

Map has the Session methods (run, add_data, layers, to_png, ...); m.session is the session itself. Files of up to 2 MB travel with the project, so the app shows them; a larger file is read from its path, which only Python can see, so it draws in to_png but not in the app. The whole project goes across after each change, so changes made on both sides at once don't merge: the later one wins. A change made in the app replaces Python's project, so m.undo() undoes only what Python did since.

The app is the web app, loaded from https://web.rustgis.app, so the notebook needs to be online. Map(url=...) or the RUSTGIS_WEB_URL environment variable points it at another copy (a self-hosted one, or trunk serve in apps/rustgis-web). Settings you change in the widget last until the cell is run again: an embedded app keeps nothing in the browser.

The project, with the data that travels with it, goes to that app through the browser (postMessage); nothing goes to a server. The app runs in your browser, so with the default address your data stays on your machine. Point url= only at a copy of the app you trust.

items.title: Commands
items.text:
Every action in RustGIS is a command with an id and JSON parameters: the same ids the ribbon, the command line and the AI Assistant use. Session.run(id, ...) runs any of them, with the parameters as keyword arguments, a dict, or both. It returns the command's result and raises rustgis.RustGISError when the command fails.

s.commands()                                        # every command, with its parameters
s.tools()                                           # the geoprocessing tools
s.run("select.byAttributes", where="pop_max > 10000000", layer="Cities")
s.run("map.goToXY", {"lon": 114.1, "lat": 22.4, "scale": 2_000_000})
s.notices()                                         # what the last commands reported
s.undo()

The GeoLibre and Whitebox tools run as they do in the app, through the geolibre program (see Analysis). rustgis.load_plugins(), or Session(plugins=True), loads the plugins installed for the desktop app.

items.title: Data in and out
items.text:
s = rustgis.Session(data=["parcels.gpkg", "roads.fgb"])   # or s.add_data(path, name=...)
s.add_geojson({"type": "FeatureCollection", "features": [...]}, name="Sites")

gdf = s.layer("Cities").to_geopandas()             # a GeoDataFrame in EPSG:4326
s.add_geopandas(gdf[gdf.pop_max > 5_000_000], name="Big cities")
s.layer("Cities").to_geojson()                     # a FeatureCollection dict

Every format the app reads works here: GeoJSON, CSV, Shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, KML/KMZ, GPX, GeoTIFF and the rest of Supported Data Formats. A large file read in place keeps only the features of the last view in memory; run layer.loadAll on it before to_geojson or to_geopandas to get all of them.

items.title: From source
items.text:
The package lives in apps/rustgis-python, built with maturin:

pip install ./apps/rustgis-python                   # or: cd apps/rustgis-python && maturin develop
python -m pytest apps/rustgis-python/tests

Its version is the RustGIS version, and each release publishes wheels to PyPI.

items.title: RustGIS vs. other GIS platforms
items.text:
How RustGIS compares to its sibling project GeoLibre and to the GIS platforms people most often ask about: QGIS, ArcGIS Pro and ArcGIS Online.

RustGIS is not trying to replace any of these. It fills a narrower spot: a free and open-source desktop GIS compiled to a single native program, with a ribbon interface familiar from desktop GIS, every action available as a scriptable command, and the same app running in a browser tab through WebAssembly.

How to read this

Comparisons like this age quickly and are written by an interested party. The RustGIS column reflects what ships in the current source as of October 2026; the other columns describe each product's mainstream, out-of-the-box behaviour, not what is reachable with every add-on or plugin. The GeoLibre, QGIS and ArcGIS columns draw on GeoLibre's own comparison, where those products are described in more depth. Found something wrong or out of date? Please open an issue.

Coming from QGIS? RustGIS and QGIS goes deeper: the pros and cons of each, how QGIS concepts map onto RustGIS, and how to use the two together. Deciding between RustGIS and its sibling? RustGIS and GeoLibre compares the two in detail.

items.title: RustGIS and GeoLibre
items.text:
RustGIS and GeoLibre are both opengeos projects, and they share more than a maintainer: both run the same suite of over 1,000 GeoLibre and Whitebox geoprocessing tools, natively on the desktop and on WebAssembly in the browser.

They differ in how they are built and who they suit:

  • GeoLibre is built on web technology (Tauri, React, MapLibre GL JS, DuckDB-WASM, deck.gl). It reaches further: cloud-native formats (GeoParquet, PMTiles, Zarr, STAC), databases, OGC and Esri services, native Android and iOS apps, a Jupyter widget, a Python package and real-time collaboration.
  • RustGIS is written entirely in Rust and draws its own interface on the GPU (egui). It is one native program with no browser engine or JavaScript runtime inside, a ribbon laid out in the order of the work, and an engine where every button is a command with an id, run the same way by the ribbon, rustgis-cli, notebooks, models and the AI Assistant.

If you want the widest data access and the most platforms, choose GeoLibre. If you want a compact native desktop GIS with a classic ribbon workflow and a fully scriptable command engine, choose RustGIS. Both keep your data on your machine. See RustGIS and GeoLibre for a closer look.

items.title: Where each one is the right choice
items.text:
Choose RustGIS when you want a compact, native desktop GIS that installs as one program, a ribbon interface without a licence, every action scriptable from the command line with the same ids the interface uses, plugins that run sandboxed, or an AI assistant whose every step is an undoable command.

Choose GeoLibre when you need the widest data access from a browser tab (cloud-native formats, STAC, databases, OGC and Esri services), the same app on Android, iOS and in Jupyter, real-time collaboration, or a Python package.

Choose QGIS when you need the widest format support through GDAL/OGR, the deepest open-source cartography, a mature plugin for a niche task, or heavy local processing of large datasets.

Choose ArcGIS Pro when you are in the Esri ecosystem, need enterprise geodatabases and versioned editing, the deepest 3D and imagery workflows, or organizational support.

Choose ArcGIS Online when the priority is hosted layers, organizational sharing and the surrounding Esri app family.

They also compose: RustGIS reads and writes GeoJSON, CSV, GeoPackage, GeoParquet, Shapefile and GeoTIFF, which every tool above opens, and writes MapLibre styles and OGC API Features collections for the web.

items.title: Where RustGIS is not the strongest option
items.text:
Stated plainly, so the tables above are worth trusting:

  • Format breadth. Databases are PostgreSQL/PostGIS (read only) and DuckDB files (through DuckDB), on the desktop, and the web app doesn't write GeoPackages. Other vector formats (File Geodatabase, DWG…) and rasters (JPEG 2000, NetCDF, HDF…) need GDAL installed, and SQL queries need DuckDB, which RustGIS calls rather than links.
  • Coordinate systems. Vector data is stored in longitude/latitude; there is no full PROJ.
  • Editing depth. No vertex editing of existing features yet, and no versioned or multi-user editing.
  • Specialized analysis. Spatial joins, overlay union and intersect, network datasets and spatial statistics are thin or missing, beyond what the GeoLibre and Whitebox tools cover.
  • Python. The rustgis package runs commands headlessly, but there is no Python console inside the app and no Python plugins.
  • Maturity. RustGIS is young. Many features are first versions; see the roadmap.

items.title: RustGIS and GeoLibre
items.text:
RustGIS and GeoLibre are sibling opengeos projects with the same maintainer, so people often ask how they differ and which to use. This page answers that: what each is built for, where each is stronger, and how to use them together. For RustGIS beside QGIS, ArcGIS Pro and ArcGIS Online as well, see the full comparison.

How to read this

This page is written by the RustGIS project. It reflects RustGIS as of October 2026 and GeoLibre 3.4 as described in its documentation, not every plugin either one can load. Both projects move quickly, so details here age fast. Found something wrong or out of date? Please open an issue.

items.title: The short answer
items.text:
GeoLibre is the broader, web-first GIS. It is built with web technology (Tauri, React, MapLibre GL JS, DuckDB-WASM, deck.gl) and runs in a browser tab with nothing installed, as a desktop app, and as native Android and iOS apps. It reaches further into data (databases, cloud catalogs, dozens of open-data portals), 3D (Cesium, 3D Tiles, I3S, Gaussian splats), AI (SAM segmentation, ONNX object detection), sharing (share links, review comments, real-time collaboration) and the Python and R ecosystems (a Jupyter widget and an R package).

RustGIS is the narrower, native one. It is a single program written entirely in Rust that draws its own interface on the GPU, with no browser engine or JavaScript runtime inside, and the same program compiled to WebAssembly for the browser. Its interface is a ribbon laid out in the order of the work, every button is a command you can run from the command line, Python or an AI agent, its plugins run sandboxed, and it goes further in the classic desktop GIS jobs of data design, reports and print layouts.

They are complementary rather than competing. Both run the same 1,000+ GeoLibre and Whitebox geoprocessing tools, both keep your data on your device, and both read and write the same open formats. Choose GeoLibre for reach, choose RustGIS for a compact, scriptable desktop GIS, or use both.

items.title: Where GeoLibre is stronger
items.text:
• More platforms. GeoLibre runs as a web app, an installable PWA, a desktop app on Windows, macOS and Linux, native Android and iOS apps, a Docker image, a Chrome extension and a Jupyter widget. RustGIS runs on the desktop and in the browser; it has no mobile app and no touch-first layout.
  • Data reach. GeoLibre opens more formats in the app itself, including File Geodatabase, DWG, MapInfo TAB, NetCDF-4/HDF5, Kerchunk and Icechunk, ICESat-2 and GEDI. It connects to SQL Server and Apache Iceberg as well as PostGIS and DuckDB, and its plugins browse dozens of catalogs and portals, from NASA Earthdata and Planet to Hugging Face and about 150 US local agencies. RustGIS reads a focused set natively and the rest through GDAL's programs when they are installed (see Data formats).
  • SQL in the browser. GeoLibre runs DuckDB Spatial, PGlite/PostGIS and Apache Sedona inside the browser. RustGIS's SQL pane uses DuckDB on the desktop; its web app has no SQL engine yet.
  • Cartography depth. GeoLibre has rule-based and expression renderers, heat maps, clustering, diagrams, blend modes, layer groups, a data-defined label engine, and style interchange with SLD, QGIS QML and Mapbox GL JSON. RustGIS covers the common renderers and collision-free labels, without that depth.
  • 3D. GeoLibre has a Cesium globe with terrain, 3D Tiles, I3S, Gaussian splats, CZML and Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles. RustGIS has a globe, 2.5D extrusion and LiDAR point layers.
  • AI and imagery models. Besides an AI assistant, GeoLibre has SAM segmentation, in-browser ONNX/YOLO object detection and an object-based image analysis workbench. RustGIS has pixel classification (k-means, minimum distance and a trainable neural network).
  • Sharing and collaboration. GeoLibre shares projects through links with roles, expiry and passwords, has review comments anchored to the map, story maps, dashboards, and an experimental real-time collaboration mode. RustGIS shares by writing files: web map pages, packages and static exports.
  • Python, R and notebooks. The geolibre Python package is a two-way Jupyter widget with a leafmap-style API, the geolibre R package works in RStudio, Quarto and Shiny, and the notebook panel runs JupyterLite or JupyterLab. RustGIS has a Python package that runs commands headlessly and built-in notebooks of command cells, but no Python console in the app and no R package.
  • Opening other projects. GeoLibre imports QGIS (.qgs/.qgz) and ArcGIS Pro (.aprx/.mapx) projects. RustGIS opens neither.
  • Editing. GeoLibre edits vertices and writes edits back to their sources (GeoPackage, PostGIS, ArcGIS feature services). RustGIS cannot yet edit the vertices of existing features, and edits stay in the project until exported.
  • Languages. GeoLibre's interface comes in 21 languages, including right-to-left Arabic, Hebrew and Persian. RustGIS has 16, none right-to-left.

items.title: Where RustGIS is stronger
items.text:
• A native program, not a web view. RustGIS is memory-safe Rust compiled to one native program (18–30 MB installers) with no browser engine, JavaScript or Python inside. Large GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf and Shapefile files are streamed a view at a time rather than loaded into a browser tab's memory, and nothing depends on a web view's limits.
  • Everything is a command. Every ribbon button, shortcut and pane action is a command with an id and JSON parameters, and the same ids run from rustgis-cli, the rustgis Python package, notebooks, models, the Script pane, the MCP server and the AI Assistant. A batch of maps can be rendered in CI with one command line. GeoLibre is driven through its interface, its Python and R packages and its MCP server; it has no general command-line tool.
  • Sandboxed plugins. RustGIS plugins are WebAssembly modules that can do only what their declared permissions allow, and the same file runs on the desktop, in rustgis-cli and in the browser. GeoLibre's TypeScript plugins can do much more inside the app (panels, map tools, custom layers), but its plugin API states that they "run as trusted code in the app window" and that its policy "is not a security boundary".
  • Data design. RustGIS defines domains, subtypes, attribute rules, contingent values, relationship classes, archiving, topology rules and traverse/COGO in the project itself, the geodatabase design work of ArcGIS Pro. GeoLibre has attribute forms with constraints and honours the domains and subtypes of the ArcGIS feature services it edits, but doesn't define its own.
  • Reports and layouts. RustGIS builds grouped reports with statistics, charts and subreports, and layouts with map frames, grids, extent indicators and map series. GeoLibre's print layout and atlas cover the common cases, and it has no report builder.
  • A ribbon interface. Tabs follow the order of the work (Home, Data, Style, Edit, Analyze, View, Publish), with Command Search (Ctrl+K) to find any command or tool by name. People coming from ArcGIS Pro often find it familiar. GeoLibre uses menus and panels, with a command palette and beginner, intermediate and advanced interface levels.
  • Self-contained. Everything RustGIS does with local data runs inside the program, with no network, server or helper process, and offline areas sync edited features back. GeoLibre works offline too, but some features need a remote host (GDAL export, ONNX detection and story map HTML export among them), and on the desktop its raster tools and some vector tools use an optional Python sidecar.
