items.title: Using them together
items.text:
The two read and write the same open formats, so data moves between them without conversion: GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, Shapefile, GeoJSON, KML/KMZ, GPX, CSV and cloud-optimised GeoTIFF. Neither opens the other's project file yet; move the data across and restyle it.

They also share their geoprocessing. RustGIS's Analyze › Tools runs the GeoLibre and Whitebox suite (natively through the geolibre program on the desktop, and on WebAssembly in the browser), so a tool learned in one works the same way in the other. See Analysis.

A common split is to explore, share and collaborate in GeoLibre, especially from a browser, a phone or a notebook, and to use RustGIS for repeatable desktop work: a project scripted command by command, maps rendered by rustgis-cli in CI, data with domains and attribute rules, or reports and map series printed to PDF.

items.title: Common questions
items.text:
Why are there two? They are built on different foundations for different jobs. GeoLibre uses the web platform to reach as many places and data sources as possible. RustGIS explores what a desktop GIS looks like as one native Rust program in which every action is a command. Each project borrows ideas from the other.

Which one should I start with? If you want to open a dataset in a browser tab or on a phone right now, or work in Jupyter or R, start with GeoLibre. If you want a desktop GIS with a ribbon, a command line that can do everything the interface can, or reports and data design, start with RustGIS.

Do they run the same geoprocessing tools? Yes: the GeoLibre and Whitebox suite of over 1,000 tools, built from geolibre-rust. RustGIS adds its own built-in vector tools and guided workflows; GeoLibre adds its Toolbox (routing, H3 grids, spatial statistics).

Can a GeoLibre plugin run in RustGIS, or the other way round? No. GeoLibre plugins are TypeScript modules for its web interface; RustGIS plugins are sandboxed WebAssembly modules that add commands and tools.

Can I open a GeoLibre project in RustGIS? Not yet. Export the layers (GeoPackage or GeoParquet keep the most) and add them to RustGIS.

items.title: RustGIS and QGIS
items.text:
"How does RustGIS compare to QGIS?" is the question people ask most. This page answers it directly: where each one is stronger, how QGIS concepts map onto RustGIS, and how to use the two together. For RustGIS beside GeoLibre, ArcGIS Pro and ArcGIS Online as well, see the full comparison.

How to read this

This page is written by the RustGIS project, so read it with that in mind. It reflects RustGIS as of October 2026 and QGIS's out-of-the-box behaviour, not everything reachable through its plugins. Found something wrong or out of date? Please open an issue.

items.title: The short answer
items.text:
QGIS is the mature, complete open-source desktop GIS. Over twenty years it has grown the widest format support (through GDAL/OGR) and full coordinate-system support (through PROJ), the deepest open-source cartography, thorough editing, GRASS and SAGA processing, QGIS Server, mobile companions (QField, Mergin Maps) and thousands of Python plugins, with a large community, training material and books behind it.

RustGIS is younger and narrower, built differently. It is one native program written entirely in Rust, an 18–30 MB download that also runs as the whole app in a browser tab. Its interface is a ribbon laid out in the order of the work, every button is a command you can run from the command line, Python or an AI agent, and its plugins run sandboxed.

RustGIS is not a QGIS replacement, and doesn't aim to be. If your work depends on what QGIS does best, keep using QGIS. RustGIS suits people who want something lighter to install, a browser version with nothing to install, a command-driven engine, or a ribbon workflow without a licence, and the two read and write the same open formats.

items.title: What they look like
items.text:
The same World Atlas data, styled the same way, in each app.

RustGIS: the ribbon, the Layers pane and the AI Assistant.

QGIS with the same data and styling: toolbars and the Browser and Layers panels.

items.title: Where RustGIS is stronger
items.text:
• Installing it. RustGIS is a single program with no Python, Qt or GDAL inside: the installers are 18–30 MB depending on the platform (a portable Windows zip, a macOS DMG, an AppImage, .deb/.rpm, Homebrew, winget, the AUR, Fedora COPR). QGIS installers bundle a Python interpreter, Qt, GDAL, GRASS and more, and run to hundreds of megabytes. See Installation.
  • In the browser. The whole app, not a viewer, is compiled to WebAssembly and runs at web.rustgis.app: add files, style them, run the 1,000+ GeoLibre and Whitebox tools, build layouts and export, with the data staying on your device. You can serve the static build yourself. QGIS has no official browser version; QGIS Server and qgis2web publish maps made on the desktop.
  • Everything is a command. Every ribbon button, shortcut and pane action is a command with an id and JSON parameters. The same ids run from rustgis-cli, the rustgis Python package, notebooks, models, the Script pane, the MCP server and the AI Assistant, so what you can click you can script, exactly. QGIS's processing algorithms are scriptable through qgis_process and PyQGIS, but much of its interface (styling, layouts, project setup) is reached through the PyQGIS object model rather than the same actions the buttons run.
  • An AI Assistant that acts through undoable commands. The AI Assistant is built in, works with Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenRouter, Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible model with your own key, and does everything through the same commands, so every step shows in History and can be undone; file, network and plugin commands wait for your approval. An MCP server lets agents such as Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code drive RustGIS. QGIS has AI through third-party plugins.
  • Sandboxed plugins. RustGIS plugins are WebAssembly modules that can do only what their declared permissions allow (editing the project, reading files, the network), and the same file runs on the desktop, in rustgis-cli and in the browser. QGIS plugins are Python with the full access of the user running QGIS: far more capable, but trusted rather than contained.
  • Cloud-native data without extra libraries. Cloud-optimised GeoTIFF, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, PMTiles and Zarr are read in place by RustGIS's own readers, over HTTP byte ranges and from s3:// buckets, on the desktop and in the browser alike. QGIS reads all of these too, through GDAL on the desktop.
  • A ribbon interface. Tabs follow the order of the work (Home, Data, Style, Edit, Analyze, View, Publish), with Command Search (Ctrl+K) to find any command or tool by name. People coming from ArcGIS Pro often find it familiar; people who know QGIS's toolbars may not want it, which is a matter of taste.
  • A permissive licence. RustGIS is Apache-2.0, so its crates can be embedded in proprietary or differently licensed software. QGIS is GPL-2.0-or-later, which requires derived works to stay under the GPL. For running either program, both are free.
  • Built not to crash. RustGIS is memory-safe Rust with no unsafe code, treats every file and parameter as hostile, and its test suite runs every command and tool with junk input to check that none of them panics.

items.title: Where QGIS is stronger
items.text:
• Format and database breadth. QGIS opens the formats its GDAL/OGR build supports, natively, and writes many of them. RustGIS reads a focused set of formats with its own code (see Data formats) and reaches the rest, such as File Geodatabase, DWG, JPEG 2000 or NetCDF, only when GDAL's programs are installed. QGIS also connects to PostGIS, SpatiaLite, Oracle and SQL Server and edits in them directly; RustGIS reads PostGIS tables live (read only) and DuckDB databases through DuckDB, on the desktop.
  • Coordinate systems. QGIS uses full PROJ: every CRS, datum transformations and grids, and layers kept in their own CRS. RustGIS holds vector coordinates as WGS 84 longitude/latitude and reprojects rasters and the map by EPSG code, which covers mapping and most analysis but not survey-grade work in a local datum.
  • Editing. QGIS has a complete digitizing toolkit: vertex editing, reshape, offset curves, advanced digitizing with constraints, topological editing, geometry checkers. RustGIS creates, moves, rotates, scales, splits and merges features with snapping and templates, but cannot yet edit the vertices of existing features.
  • Processing. Both have over 1,000 tools, but they differ. QGIS combines its native algorithms with GDAL, GRASS and SAGA providers, and covers vector analysis RustGIS is thin on: spatial joins, intersect and union overlays, network analysis on real road graphs, spatial statistics. RustGIS's breadth comes mostly from the GeoLibre and Whitebox suite, which is strong on terrain, hydrology, LiDAR and image analysis.
  • Cartography. QGIS's styling is the richest in open source: rule-based renderers, data-defined overrides on nearly every property through its expression engine, blending modes, geometry generators, a refined labeling engine. RustGIS covers the common renderers (single, unique values, graduated, proportional, aggregation, raster stretch/RGB/classified/hillshade) and collision-free labels, without that depth.
  • Print layouts. QGIS's layout designer and atlas are mature and detailed. RustGIS has map frames, legends, scale bars, grids, map series, reports and PDF export, as first versions.
  • Plugins and integrations. QGIS has thousands of Python plugins for niche tasks, an in-app Python console, QGIS Server for OGC services, and QField and Mergin Maps for field work. RustGIS's plugin registry is new and small, and it has no server or mobile app.
  • 3D and point clouds. QGIS's 3D map views, mesh layers and point-cloud rendering go further than RustGIS's globe, 2.5D extrusion and LiDAR point layers.
  • Maturity and community. QGIS has two decades of releases, a long-term-release cycle, translated documentation, courses, books, user groups and commercial support. RustGIS released its first version in 2026; many features are first versions and some workflows will have gaps. See the roadmap.

items.title: Using them together
items.text:
You don't have to choose. RustGIS reads and writes the formats QGIS works in, so data moves between them without conversion:

  • Vector data: GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, Shapefile, GeoJSON, KML/KMZ, GPX and CSV, in both directions.
  • Rasters: GeoTIFF and cloud-optimised GeoTIFF.
  • Colour ramps: RustGIS reads QGIS Style Manager exports (.xml) and the colour ramp or raster colour map in a layer style (.qml); see Custom color ramps.
  • Web maps: MapLibre styles and OGC API Features collections exported from RustGIS can be served and opened anywhere, QGIS included.

RustGIS does not open QGIS project files (.qgz) or full QGIS layer styles; move the data across and restyle it.

A common split is to do heavy editing, PROJ-dependent work and detailed cartography in QGIS, and use RustGIS where a light install, the browser, scripting by command id or the AI Assistant helps: a quick look at a GeoParquet on a laptop without QGIS, a map shared as a web app, a batch of maps rendered by rustgis-cli in CI, or the 1,000+ GeoLibre and Whitebox tools from a browser tab.

items.title: Common questions
items.text:
Is RustGIS a replacement for QGIS? No. It covers the everyday work of a desktop GIS (adding data, styling, labelling, geoprocessing, layouts, sharing) and does some things QGIS doesn't, but QGIS is far more complete. Use RustGIS alongside QGIS, or instead of it only if the gaps above don't touch your work.

Is RustGIS faster than QGIS? It starts quickly and is light to install, and its own readers draw large cloud-native files a view at a time. We haven't published benchmarks against QGIS, and speed depends on the data and the task, so try your own data in both.

Can I use my QGIS plugins in RustGIS? No. QGIS plugins are Python written against PyQGIS. RustGIS plugins are sandboxed WebAssembly modules; see Plugins for writing one.

Does RustGIS need GDAL like QGIS does? No. Its common formats, cloud-native formats and GeoTIFF are read by its own Rust code, which is also why the browser version works. GDAL is optional: when its programs are installed, RustGIS uses them for the formats it doesn't read itself.

Can I open a QGIS project? Not yet. Open the project's data in RustGIS (GeoPackage is the easiest route) and restyle it.

items.title: The window
items.text:
• Ribbon: tabs of commands grouped by task. The Project button opens the backstage (new, open, save, About).
  • Quick Access Toolbar (top left): New, Open, Save, Undo and Redo, plus any commands you add under Settings › Customize › Quick Access.
  • Layers pane (left): the map's layers in drawing order, with their legends. Tick a layer to show or hide it; drag it up or down to change the drawing order; right-click it to zoom to it, rename or remove it and more. Type in the box at the top to show only the layers and tables whose names contain the text (Esc clears it); a selected layer it hides is no longer selected, and layers can be reordered again once it is cleared. The buttons beside the list's title list the layers by drawing order, by data source (grouped under the file, web address or database each comes from) or by selection (selectable layers first, each with a box to make it selectable or not and its count of selected features); only the drawing order reorders layers. A layer that isn't selectable is skipped by the Select tool's clicks and boxes on the map; Select By Attributes, Select Layer By Location and the attribute table still select in it, since they name the layer. The Style and Data tabs act on the layer selected here. The tabs at the top of the left pane switch it between Layers, Browser and Data Sources (also in View › Windows).
  • Map view: one tab per map and layout. The buttons at the top right zoom in, zoom out and go to the full extent; the north arrow and scale bar sit in the corners; tile credits at the bottom right.
  • Panes (right): Catalog, Geoprocessing, Symbology, History, Details, Editing, Workflows, Script, the AI Assistant and more. Open them from View › Windows or the commands that use them. Each pane opened gets a tab at the top, in the order opened: click a tab to show its pane, and its ✕ to close it (the next tab shows; closing the last hides the side). Right-click a tab to close it, the others or all; the ✕ at the header's end closes every pane. Tabs that don't fit are listed under ». A ribbon button for a pane shows it when it is open but not in view, and closes it when it is. Pane Sets keep the tabs open.
  • Status bar: the scale (type one, or pick from the list), the coordinate system (click it to change the projection), the pointer's coordinates (click them to switch between decimal degrees and DMS), the selection count and the draw time.

Command Search (Ctrl+K, or the box at the top right) finds any command or geoprocessing tool by name and runs it.

To give the map more room, collapse the ribbon to its tab row with the chevron at its right end, by double-clicking a tab, or with Ctrl+F1 (Cmd+F1 on macOS, where F1 may need the Fn key). Click a tab to peek at its commands while collapsed. When the window is narrower than the ribbon, arrows at its ends scroll it.

items.title: Projects
items.text:
A project (.rgis) holds maps, layouts, reports, presentations, notebooks, styles, tasks and models. Vector data added from files is stored inside the project, so a project file is self-contained; rasters are referenced by path on the desktop and stored inside the project in the web app. Project › New starts a blank map or the World Atlas sample; Save and Save As write the project, named after its file; a project opened from a file is named after that file too. See Project items for the other files RustGIS reads and writes.

Every change is a command, and every command can be undone (Ctrl+Z) and redone (Ctrl+Y).

items.title: Selection and queries
items.text:
Home › Select picks features by clicking or dragging a box (Shift adds, Ctrl removes). It takes only features that are drawn, in selectable layers: a definition query or a display filter hiding a feature keeps it out, and a click picks the feature drawn on top among the selectable layers. Select By Attributes takes a SQL clause and checks it as you type; Select By Location picks features that touch another layer's features or lie within a search distance of them (or, inverted, those that don't). Selected features draw in cyan and are highlighted in the attribute table, and the selection is synced both ways. Switch, clear or zoom to the selection, or make a new layer from it.

Select By Attributes and definition queries use SQL WHERE clauses:

pop_est > 100000000 AND continent = 'Asia'
name LIKE 'S%'
iso_a3 IN ('FRA', 'DEU', 'ITA')
gdp_md IS NULL
"OR" = 1          -- double quotes name a field, even a keyword

items.title: Geoprocessing tools
items.text:
Open a tool from the Analyze tab's gallery, Analyze › Tools (the Tools pane, which searches every tool) or Command Search. Fill in its parameters and click Run: the result is added to the map, and the run is listed under Analyze › History. From the command line or a script (gp.run), a built-in tool's parameter with a list of choices, such as Buffer's units, takes one of them in any letter case ("meters" for Meters); any other value is an error that names the choices (Buffer's units no longer take the abbreviations m, mi or metres). The built-in tools:

Tool Toolbox Buffer Analysis › Proximity Clip, Erase Analysis › Extract / Overlay Dissolve Data Management › Generalization Minimum Bounding Geometry, Feature To Point, XY Table To Point, Calculate Geometry Attributes Data Management › Features Simplify Cartography › Generalization Select Layer By Location / Attribute Data Management › Layers and Table Views Summarize Within, Summary Statistics Analysis › Summarize / Statistics Export Features Conversion IDW Interpolation Analysis › Interpolation

Tools honour the current selection: with features selected, only those are processed.

IDW Interpolation works like the QGIS tool of the same name: every point weighs on every cell by 1/distanceᴾ, where P is the distance coefficient (2 by default). Lines and polygons contribute their vertices. Leave the extent empty to use the input's, or give it as xmin,ymin,xmax,ymax in degrees. The result is a Float32 GeoTIFF layer.

items.title: GeoLibre tools
items.text:
The desktop app and the command line can also run the GeoLibre tool suite: over 1,000 tools from Whitebox and GeoLibre for terrain analysis (slope, aspect, hillshade, curvature), hydrology (fill depressions, flow direction and accumulation, watersheds), image processing, interpolation and vector work. They run on the map's layers and add their outputs as new layers.

The suite is an optional download, so RustGIS itself stays small: the GeoLibre runner, a single geolibre program (about 20 MB to download). In the Tools pane, click Install GeoLibre tools under GeoLibre tools: RustGIS downloads the latest runner for your platform from the geolibre-rust releases, checks it against its published SHA-256 checksum (which catches a corrupted download; the release itself is trusted as when you download it by hand) and installs it in its data folder (~/.local/share/rustgis/geolibre on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/RustGIS/geolibre on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\RustGIS\geolibre on Windows). From the command line, gp.installGeolibre does the same.

To remove it, click Uninstall beside GeoLibre at the top of the Tools pane, then Confirm uninstall (gp.uninstallGeolibre from the command line): RustGIS deletes its geolibre data folder. A runner you located yourself, or one on your PATH, is not deleted; RustGIS goes on using it. You can install the tools again at any time. In the browser, Remove unloads the tools and stops loading them when RustGIS starts.

To install it yourself instead, download the archive for your platform (geolibre-<version>-<platform>.tar.gz, or .zip on Windows), unpack it anywhere, and click Locate… to pick the geolibre program; RustGIS remembers it.

RustGIS also finds the runner without asking when it is next to the RustGIS program (or in a geolibre folder beside it), on your PATH, or named by the RUSTGIS_GEOLIBRE environment variable (the command line uses these). The tools then appear under GeoLibre in the Tools pane and the Browser's toolboxes, grouped by the category and subcategory the runner gives each tool (Conversion, Hydrology, LiDAR, Projection, Raster, Remote Sensing, Terrain, Vector, then e.g. GeoLibre › Terrain › Derivatives). A runner too old to list subcategories groups them by category only. Find Tools searches them.

  • Raster inputs are passed as their own files; vector layers (or their selection) are written in the first raster input's coordinate system, or the UTM zone around the data, so distances and areas are in metres. Data spanning more than 40° of longitude stays in degrees.
  • Tools that take several layers (a composite's bands, a mosaic's tiles) list them in order: Add picks a layer, and ▲ ▼ change its place (the order of the bands, for a composite). From the command line, name them separated by ;: "inputs":"red;green;blue". In the desktop app a file not open as a layer can be added too: type its path below the list and press Enter.
  • Raster outputs are kept inside the project, so they save and reopen with it. Text and table reports appear in the tool's messages.
  • LiDAR and other inputs RustGIS doesn't open as layers take a file path, read like Add Data reads one. Outputs are written to a fresh scratch folder and loaded from there.
  • Each run is a separate geolibre process, so a tool that fails can't take RustGIS down.
  • From the command line: gp.run={"tool":"geolibre:slope","params":{"input":"dem"}}; gp.tools lists every tool's parameters, gp.geolibre shows the runner in use and gp.setGeolibre={"path":"…"} picks one.

In the web app, click Load GeoLibre tools in the Tools pane instead. RustGIS loads geolibre-rust's WebAssembly runner (the geolibre-wasm package, from jsDelivr, about 25 MB the first time, then from the browser's cache) and the tools run in the page, in an in-memory folder: nothing is uploaded. The web app remembers this and loads them again on your next visit. The runner's code comes from jsDelivr, pinned to one geolibre-wasm release, the same trust as installing that package. Tools that read files by path (LiDAR files, for instance) need the desktop app, since a web page has no file system.

In the desktop app and on the command line, RustGIS waits while a tool runs, so a long run on a large raster or point cloud keeps the window busy until it finishes. In the web app the run is started in the background and the result is added when it ends, but the tool itself runs in the page, so the page is busy while it computes.

items.title: Analysis workflows
items.text:
The Analyze tab's Workflows pane holds guided analyses. Where one needs points, it asks you to click them on the map:

Workflow What it does Raster Functions Slope, aspect, hillshade, NDVI, band math ((b4-b3)/(b4+b3)), thresholds, resampling Function Editor Chains raster functions, each on the previous output Suitability Modeler Scores rasters 1–10 and adds them with weights Visibility Analysis A viewshed from a point on an elevation raster Exploratory 3D Analysis A line of sight between two points, split into seen and hidden parts Geostatistical Wizard An IDW surface from point values Network Analysis The shortest (or cheapest, by a cost field) route over a line layer Neighborhood Explorer What lies within a distance of a point, with sums of numeric fields Simulation Random points in polygons (a fixed number, or from a field × rate) Data Engineering Counts, nulls, distinct values, min, max and mean of every field Exploratory Analysis Histograms and correlations of numeric fields Embeddings The features most like the selected one, by their numeric attributes Data Interop KML, GPX, CSV with WKT, GeoJSON or CSV

Rasters these make are kept in the project. Environments limit tools to the map view, the full extent or everywhere, and set the cell size of new rasters. ModelBuilder chains tools into models (a parameter %1 is step 1's output), and New Model From History turns the geoprocessing you've run into a model. The Script pane runs commands from text, one per line (id {json}).

items.title: Imagery
items.text:
The Analyze tab's imagery groups open their tools in the Workflows pane:

  • Ortho Mapping and Reality Mapping workspaces mosaic georeferenced images into an orthomosaic, or elevation rasters into a surface model that exports as a 3D mesh (OBJ).
  • Georeference places a raster from control points (column, row, longitude, latitude) or stretches it over the map view.
  • Change Detection (difference, ratio, percent), Spectral Analysis (every band at a pixel), Indices (NDVI, NDWI, SAVI, NBR, NDBI, EVI), Process (clip to the view, resample) and the Pixel Editor (set the pixels inside a polygon).
  • Classification Wizard (unsupervised k-means) and Classification Tools (minimum distance from training polygons).
  • Mensuration: distances along the surface, heights between two points, areas, and volumes above or below a base height, with a list of results.

items.title: Deep learning and hosted imagery
items.text: Analyze › Deep Learning Tools trains a neural network (a multilayer perceptron) on the pixels under training polygons and classifies every pixel, adding a class raster with a confidence band and reporting the accuracy on held-back pixels. Trained models stay in the project; Share › Package › Deep Learning saves one as a package to apply in other projects. Analyze › Create Hosted Imagery cuts a raster into XYZ web map tiles (PNG, transparent outside the raster) with a TileJSON file and a viewer page.

items.title: AI Assistant
items.text:
Analyze › AI Assistant (also View › Windows, or Command Search) opens a chat pane. Ask a question about your data or say what to do with the map, and the assistant answers by running RustGIS commands and geoprocessing tools for you:

  • "Which 5 countries have the largest GDP?" reads the Countries table and answers.
  • "Label the cities with their names, and zoom to Tokyo."
  • "Buffer the cities by 200 km and colour the result by population."
  • "Switch to a dark basemap and hide the rivers."

Each step it takes shows in the conversation (click one to see its parameters and result), and each change is one undo step, so Ctrl+Z takes back anything you don't want. It never says it changed the map unless a command succeeded. Commands that would read or write files, connect to an address on the internet, run a plugin, script or task, or replace the project wait for you: Allow or Decline. File and network access can be allowed for the rest of the conversation, for that exact command and file or address only. Enter sends, Shift+Enter starts a new line, Up and Down recall earlier messages, and Stop ends a run.

From the command line, rustgis-cli ask sends one request (see Command Line).

items.title: Choosing a model
items.text:
Click the model name or the gear to open the settings. The assistant works with:

Provider Default model Key Anthropic claude-opus-5-5 console.anthropic.com, or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY OpenAI gpt-5.5 platform.openai.com, or OPENAI_API_KEY ChatGPT (sign in) the first model in your account’s current catalog none: Continue with ChatGPT to use your ChatGPT plan (desktop app and command line) Google Gemini gemini-3.8-flash aistudio.google.com, or GEMINI_API_KEY / GOOGLE_API_KEY OpenRouter openrouter/auto openrouter.ai, or OPENROUTER_API_KEY Ollama (local) qwen3 none; the server from OLLAMA_BASE_URL (default http://localhost:11434) OpenAI-compatible — LM Studio, vLLM, llama.cpp…: the address from OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_BASE_URL, an optional OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_KEY

The ↻ button lists the provider's models. The provider and model you last chose in the settings are used at start. Until you choose one, RUSTGIS_ASSISTANT_PROVIDER and RUSTGIS_ASSISTANT_MODEL pick them, and otherwise the desktop uses the first provider with a key in the environment. Saved settings win over the environment. Models that call tools well give the best results; small local models may stop early or skip steps.

items.title: Signing in with ChatGPT
items.text:
With a ChatGPT plan you can use the assistant without an API key, through OpenAI's Sign in with ChatGPT for open-source apps. Choose ChatGPT (sign in) and click Continue with ChatGPT: your browser opens OpenAI's sign-in page, where you approve RustGIS using your plan (the first time, OpenAI registers RustGIS as an app of your account; you can rename it there). Afterwards the settings show the account's email, Using ChatGPT plan, and a Weekly usage link to your ChatGPT usage settings, where you can see and limit what RustGIS uses or disconnect it. Sign out clears local tokens and attempts to revoke the remote session. If OpenAI does not confirm revocation, RustGIS says so; disconnect RustGIS in ChatGPT settings to ensure that remote access ends. The registration remains for signing in again. The account picker retains separate registrations, even when their emails match. Use another account adds a registration; choose an existing one to reuse its issued client ID. From the command line:

rustgis-cli ask --login                 # continue with ChatGPT in the browser
rustgis-cli ask --login --another-account  # or register RustGIS for another account
rustgis-cli ask --sample --provider chatgpt "Zoom to Tokyo"
rustgis-cli ask --accounts              # list saved registrations
rustgis-cli ask --account oaiapp_...      # select one by its issued client id
rustgis-cli ask --login --account oaiapp_... # reauthorize that registration
rustgis-cli ask --logout

The model catalog loads after sign-in, on startup when signed in, and when switching to this provider or another account. The first model is chosen when the current one is not offered. The ↻ button reloads the catalog. The CLI uses the catalog's first model unless --model or RUSTGIS_ASSISTANT_MODEL is set. While waiting for sign-in, Open browser again and Copy sign-in link let you recover a closed tab or failed browser launch. Requests go to the OpenAI API (https://api.openai.com/v1/responses) and use your plan's usage; when a limit is reached, the assistant says so and points to the usage settings. Signing in needs the desktop app or the command line (it runs a short-lived server on 127.0.0.1, port 1455 when it's free, for the browser to return to); the web app doesn't offer it.

Live testing of this integration was limited to a ChatGPT Pro account on Windows 11. Plus, Team/Business, Enterprise and Edu accounts, macOS and Linux have not been live-verified. Plus has a five-hour usage limit shared across apps using the plan. Team/Business, Enterprise and Edu workspace policy may block plan usage. Eligibility and model catalogs depend on the selected account and workspace.

Weekly usage opens ChatGPT's settings page. RustGIS does not show a live percentage: there is no documented usage endpoint, and the tested live responses supplied no rate-limit headers.

items.title: Tool output limits
items.text:
The assistant can search_docs and read_doc to look up RustGIS features and commands. Each tool result defaults to an estimated 10,000 tokens, following Codex's default output budget. A result is capped at an absolute 24,000 tokens. Like Codex's truncation utilities, the budget uses a byte-based estimate (four UTF-8 bytes per token), rather than an exact tokenizer. It includes JSON escaping and truncation metadata. This bounds individual results, not the entire conversation or all results from a batch.

RUSTGIS_ASSISTANT_TOOL_OUTPUT_TOKEN_LIMIT changes the requested per-tool budget; it cannot bypass the 24,000-token ceiling. Embedding callers can set Config::tool_output_token_limit. MCP uses the 10,000-token default.

Oversized successful results return an explicit, bounded text preview inside valid JSON, preserving the beginning and end; ask for fewer rows or a narrower search to get complete structured data. Documentation reads preserve complete lines and return next_offset when more remain: call read_doc again with the same page/section and that offset. limit defaults to 2000 lines, following Pi's line-oriented read convention. Invalid offsets (including zero, negative numbers, fractions and strings) return an error. Tiny output budgets use minimal truncation metadata or a diagnostic string prefix rather than returning bare null; extremely small budgets can only retain an abbreviated marker. Reading a section avoids loading an entire page. A single line that cannot fit produces an explicit error rather than silently skipping text.

items.title: Skills
items.text:
Skills are instructions for a kind of task. The assistant sees only each skill's name and a line on when to use it, and reads its instructions on demand, so skills cost little until used. Loaded instructions share the configured tool-output budget; oversized results are explicitly marked as truncated. Split long skills or raise that limit (up to its existing ceiling) when complete instructions do not fit. RustGIS comes with these:

Skill For thematic-map Styling a layer by its data (graduated colours, categories, proportional symbols), labelling it and exporting the map explore-data What's in a layer: fields, value ranges, top records, counts, filters and summary statistics print-layout A page layout with a map frame, title, legend, north arrow and scale bar, exported to PDF or PNG geoprocessing Running and chaining tools: buffer, clip, erase, dissolve, select by location, summarize within add-data Adding files, web addresses, DuckDB SQL queries, STAC catalogs and Overture Maps share-web-map Sharing the map or a layer as files that work without a server: a web map, a web layer, a style, an image

The settings' Skills list shows every skill and where it comes from, with a switch to turn each one on or off:

  • Built in: the skills above.
  • Plugins: skills a plugin carries, named <plugin>:<skill>, while the plugin is enabled (see Plugins).
  • Yours: on the desktop, Add skill… adds a SKILL.md, a skill's folder, a folder of skills or a .zip of them. They are kept in the skills folder of the app's settings folder (Open folder), and Remove deletes one's SKILL.md (files you keep beside it stay). A skill of yours replaces a built-in one of the same name.
  • Shared: skills in ~/.agents/skills, where other AI agents keep theirs. They are listed but off until you turn them on, since they were written for other tools.

A skill's description and instructions reach the model as instructions you trust, like a message of your own, so turn on only skills you trust. Whatever a skill says, the commands that need your approval (files, the network, plugins) still ask.

A skill is a folder holding SKILL.md in the Agent Skills format: front matter giving its name (lower-case letters, digits and hyphens) and a description that says when to use it, then the instructions in Markdown. The assistant reads only SKILL.md. Descriptions can be single-line values or indented blocks introduced by > or |. For a description spanning several lines, use a block; plain multiline YAML values are not supported.

---
name: flood-map
description: Map flood depth and extent from a depth raster and the river network.
---

# Flood map

1. ...

From the command line:

rustgis-cli skills                      # every skill, where it comes from, and whether it's on
rustgis-cli skills add ./flood-map      # a SKILL.md, a folder or a .zip
rustgis-cli skills disable explore-data # enable / disable / remove <name>

items.title: Skill folders and ZIP names
items.text:
Skill folders may be symbolic links, including shared ~/.agents/skills folders. Enabling a shared skill trusts the instructions at that linked location; shared skills are off by default. The SKILL.md file itself must be a regular file, not a symbolic link. Removing one of your skills removes its SKILL.md, including from a linked folder's target; it does not remove the folder link or other files.

ZIP imports recognize SKILL.md regardless of letter case and accept slash or backslash path separators. Paths that collide after separator/case normalization are refused. Nested skills remain part of their containing skill. Entries are read in memory, never extracted as paths. The ZIP dependency is native-only; browser builds do not include the installer.

Skill front matter supports top-level name and description fields, plain or single/double- quoted one-line values, and indented >/| description blocks (joined into one line). This reader implements those forms rather than full YAML: trailing inline comments, multiline quoted scalars, escapes, anchors and advanced block modifiers are not interpreted. Keep comments on their own lines and put literal # text inside the intended value. Descriptions are collapsed to one whitespace-separated line before catalog insertion. On Windows, reserved device names such as con, nul, com1 and lpt1 cannot be installed; rename the skill. Unknown-name errors show up to 20 names; Settings shows the full available list.

An archive with SKILL.md at its root represents that one outermost skill: nested SKILL.md files belong to its examples/references and are not installed separately. To import several skills, put each in a sibling folder and omit a root SKILL.md. A failure during the final rename phase can leave earlier skills installed; the error names those completed installs.

items.title: Agents on this computer
items.text:
On the desktop, the assistant can hand a task to a coding agent you already have, such as Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, Cursor, OpenCode or goose. RustGIS talks to it through the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), as code editors do. The agent works on the map open here through RustGIS's tools, and with its own: calling a web API RustGIS doesn't have, running a script, writing files. It suits tasks RustGIS's own tools can't do.

It is off until you turn it on: in the settings, tick Let the assistant hand tasks to agents on this computer. The settings list the agents found. Starting a task or sending a follow-up waits for your approval in the assistant, unless automatic approval is enabled. Then ask, for example: "Have Claude Code fetch the USGS stream gauges in Texas and add them to the map."

  • It works in the background. The assistant hands over the task and carries on talking with you. A small window shows what the agent says and does until it finishes; its report then comes back into the conversation, and the assistant tells you what came of it. Several agents can work at once, each in a thread of its own (codex-1, claude-code-2…), listed above the message box with Show, Hide and × to close one.
  • Threads take follow-ups. A thread that has finished waits for more, with what it did in its context: "Now colour the gauges by flow" goes to the same agent. Threads end with New conversation, when you close them, or after half an hour of waiting.
  • You approve what it does. Each action the agent asks to take (a command, a web request, a file it writes) waits for Allow, Always allow (when the agent offers it) or Decline in its window. Allow never becomes a persistent approval: if no once-only option exists, use the explicitly labelled Always allow or decline. Approve agents' actions without asking lets them through instead. Turn it on only if you trust the agent with your computer.
  • RustGIS checks its own tools. File, network, plugin-command and project-replacement requests from a local agent wait for a separate Allow or Decline in its window. Approval applies only to that exact MCP message and that agent's run; a batch is approved or declined as a whole. The agent's --yes and the general relay checkbox cannot bypass this queue. Requests that expire, or whose agent ends, never run. Plugin management, scripts and other user-only commands remain unavailable through MCP. Approve agents' actions without asking explicitly bypasses this queue for these local agents and allows subsequent delegations without confirmation; turn it on only if you trust the agent and its inputs. It also selects the agent's own full-access mode where available.
  • Its work is kept. Each task gets a folder in Documents/RustGIS/Agent work, and what the agent adds to the map comes from there. The assistant's reply names the folder.
  • On the map, it has its thread's permission only. It reaches the map through the MCP relay with a token of its own, which RustGIS revokes when the thread ends. Stop in its window, or × in the list, revokes its token immediately and terminates its live process tree on a background thread. A reaped leader's old process ID is never signalled.
  • No console windows. On Windows, agents start without a terminal window; their window in RustGIS shows what they do.
  • Signing in is the agent's. The agent uses its own account and sign-in. If it isn't signed in, sign in with it once (for example, codex login).
  • Claude Code and Codex need Node.js. They speak ACP through an adapter (@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp, @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp), which npx downloads from npm the first time, at the version RustGIS names. Agents with ACP built in need nothing more. The web app doesn't offer agents.

items.title: Privacy
items.text:
Requests go from RustGIS straight to the provider you chose, with your key. They carry your messages, the map's layer names, fields and extent, and any rows the assistant reads to answer you; nothing goes anywhere else. A key typed in the settings is used for the session only unless you tick Remember the key on this computer, which saves it unencrypted in the app's preferences (in the browser's storage on the web); keys from the environment are never saved. A ChatGPT sign-in is kept in chatgpt-auth.json in the app's settings folder (owner-only on macOS and Linux; on Windows, protected like the rest of your user profile), never in the preferences or a project file, and its tokens are never logged; RustGIS renews them as they expire. The ChatGPT provider's address is fixed, so only the OpenAI API receives them. Renewals are serialized across RustGIS processes (a refresh token can be used only once). Plain HTTP is only used for servers on your computer or local network.

In the web app, the browser calls the provider directly. Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and OpenRouter accept that; a local Ollama server must allow the page's origin (OLLAMA_ORIGINS=https://web.rustgis.app ollama serve).

items.title: Retries and long conversations
items.text:
Live streaming text is available on the desktop. The browser currently buffers the complete response (up to the response limit, 64 MiB for SSE) before displaying it; it has no live streaming preview. Cross-origin retry timing headers are available only when the provider exposes them through CORS; otherwise ordinary backoff applies.

A failed compaction shows an error and keeps the original conversation, then stops. It does not retry continuously in the background. Sending another message or pressing Compact explicitly tries again; if the history still cannot fit, use New conversation or choose another model.

Connection failures and explicit provider overload/rate-limit failures are retried at most three times, including errors reported inside an HTTP-200 stream. The failed reply and its preview are discarded before retrying; no tool calls from it run. Usage limits, authentication failures, browser fetch failures (which can be permanent CORS refusals), timeouts and interrupted streams without an explicit retryable provider error stop without replay. Stop cancels a pending retry.

Summary requests have a total input bound, retaining the newest history if older text must be omitted. If the provider rejects a summary as too long, RustGIS halves that bound and tries again, down to 1,024 bytes; further failure stops and preserves the original conversation. This learned bound lasts for the conversation. A cut, refused or failed summary never replaces history. The summariser treats retrieved text as data, not instructions. Internal summary markers in user messages are escaped in model input; the visible transcript keeps the user's exact text.

Background agent reports are quoted as untrusted data, with markup escaped and the report payload constrained by the configured tool-output budget. The main assistant uses observations relevant to your task, rather than treating a report as a new user instruction.

ACP input uses a bounded background writer queue, so a stalled agent cannot block permission buttons or follow-up submission. Queue overflow reports an error instead of blocking. On Linux and macOS, an exited leader is observed without reaping until cleanup; its reserved identity lets Stop terminate surviving process-group descendants before finally reaping the leader.

items.title: Symbology
items.text:
Select a layer in Layers and open Style › Symbology (or the Symbology pane):

  • Single Symbol: one fill, outline and marker for every feature.
  • Unique Values: one colour per distinct value of a field. The Layers pane and layout legends list only the classes that drawn features use (after the definition query and display filters); <all other values> appears only when a drawn feature falls outside the classes and its symbol is not fully transparent. A layout legend can leave it out with Hide other values (see Layouts).
  • Graduated Colors: 1 to 12 classes of a numeric field by natural breaks (Jenks), equal interval or quantile.
  • Proportional Symbols: point size grows with a numeric field.

Pick a colour scheme from the pane's swatches. The Style tab sets the fill Color, the Outline width, Transparency and a Visibility Range (the scales between which the layer draws); points can be circles, squares, triangles, diamonds or stars. Data › Definition Query draws only the features matching a SQL clause; Unique Values, Graduated Colors and Proportional Symbols take their values, classes and sizes from those features when you apply them (apply the symbology again after changing the query), and Full Extent zooms to them. A layer with subtypes can be symbolized by them. Style › Styles saves symbology as styles to reuse on other layers and in other projects.

items.title: Edit a class
items.text:
With Unique Values or Graduated Colors, each class in the Symbology pane's list has a colour button and a legend label. Pick a colour to give that class its own. Type a label to show in the Layers pane and in layout legends instead of the value or range (for example High income for 1. High income: OECD); clear it to show the value again. <all other values> can be edited the same way. Applying the symbology again on the same field keeps the colours, outlines and labels you set by hand on the classes that are still there (the others take the scheme's colours again); picking another colour scheme recolours every class but keeps the labels. A Graduated Colors class keeps its colour and label while its range stays the same. By command:

layer.classStyle={"layer":"Countries","value":"1. High income: OECD","color":"#2E6B4F","label":"High income"}
layer.classStyle={"layer":"Countries","index":0,"label":"Under 1 million"}
layer.classStyle={"layer":"Countries","other":true,"label":"No data"}

value names a Unique Values class, index a Graduated Colors class (0 is the lowest) and other the <all other values> class; outline sets a class's outline colour. A polygon class keeps its own transparency (the layer's, as a colour scheme leaves it), so the AA of a #RRGGBBAA colour applies to points and lines only.

items.title: Custom color ramps
items.text:
Besides the built-in color schemes, a project can hold your own color ramps: an organization's palette, a published scheme such as a ColorBrewer, cmocean or viridis ramp, or one designed in a tool like Phosphor. Add them from a color ramp file with Style › Styles › Add Color Ramp File (or Add Color Ramp File under the swatches in the Symbology pane). They appear under Custom in the Symbology pane, for feature layers and rasters (Stretch, Classify, Unique Values and Shaded Relief) alike, and under Color Ramps in the Browser, where right-click deletes one. Publish › Save As › Color Ramps saves the project's custom ramps to a file.

A color ramp file (.rgisramp) is JSON: a list of ramps (or one ramp on its own), each with a name, a kind (sequential, the default, diverging or qualitative) and its stops:

[{
  "name": "Phosphor Frostfire",
  "kind": "diverging",
  "stops": ["#eff6ff", "#abc5e8", "#87a0d7", "#7b5ca6", "#ca7482", "#f5b88e", "#fff5da"]
}]

Stops are #RRGGBB or #RRGGBBAA colors, evenly spaced from the first to the last. For uneven spacing, give a stop as {"pos": 0.25, "color": "#87a0d7"}, with pos from 0 to 1; plain stops between two positioned ones are spaced evenly between them. A ramp has 2 to 256 stops (a qualitative one can have 1), and can't take the name of a built-in scheme; adding a ramp with the name of one already in the project replaces it. Scripts, the CLI and the AI Assistant add ramps with the ramp.add command ({"path": "ramps.rgisramp"}, or the JSON itself as {"text": …}), and then name them like built-in schemes, for example layer.ramp={"ramp":"Phosphor Frostfire"}.

items.title: Color ramps from other tools
items.text:
Add Color Ramp File also reads the color ramp files other tools write, so a palette from QGIS, GDAL, GMT or a tool like Phosphor can be added without converting it first:

Format Extension What RustGIS reads QGIS style .xml Every gradient ramp (discrete ones as steps) and preset ramp (as a qualitative ramp) in a Style Manager export, with its name. ColorBrewer, cpt-city and random ramps hold no colors and are skipped. QGIS layer style .qml The layer's color ramp, or a raster's color map. GDAL color-relief text .txt value R G B [A] lines (as gdaldem color-relief takes them), separated by spaces, tabs, commas or colons; values may be percentages and colors may be names; nv lines are skipped. A QGIS color map export reads the same way. GMT palette .cpt z0 color0 z1 color1 lines, with colors as r/g/b, r g b, #RRGGBB, grey levels, names or HSV; B, F and N lines are skipped.

These formats tie colors to data values; the ramp keeps their spacing, from the lowest value to the highest, and a sharp change between two colors stays sharp. A ramp from a GDAL or GMT file is named after the file and is sequential; the ramp.add command takes a name and a kind to change that ({"path": "relief.cpt", "kind": "diverging"}), and a format (rgisramp, qgis, gdal or cpt) for text without a file name. A file with more than 256 colors is resampled to 256 evenly spaced stops.

Sequential and diverging ramps blend between their stops; when there are as many classes as stops, each class takes a stop's color exactly, so a stepped palette keeps its colors. A qualitative ramp gives each class the next stop, starting again after the last. A layer keeps its own copy of the ramp it uses, so layer files, map files and packages keep their colors in projects that don't have the ramp, and deleting a ramp from the project leaves layers that use it unchanged.

items.title: Labeling
items.text:
Turn labels on per layer (View › Labeling › Label, or the Style tab), then:

  • Visibility Range: draw labels only between two scales (Out Beyond / In Beyond), or between two viewing distances (Closest / Farthest). Clear Limits removes all four.
  • Placement: automatic (above points, centred on lines and polygons), centred, or one of eight positions around the feature.
  • Lock keeps the labelled features fixed while you pan and zoom; Pause stops drawing labels for faster navigation; View Unplaced draws the labels that didn't fit in red.
  • Convert turns a layer's labels into an annotation layer: one point per label, carrying its text in a TEXT field, which you can then edit, move or delete like any other features.

items.title: Layer effects
items.text: These draw on top of the symbology. On the Style tab: Masking shows a layer only inside another layer's polygons; Display Filters show different features at different scales (a SQL condition per scale range); Aggregation draws points as hexagon or square bins coloured by count; Extrusion raises polygons by a height or a numeric field in an oblique 2.5D view, with Face Culling, Lighting (walls shaded by the way they face the light) and Cast Shadow. On the Raster Layer tab: Layer Blend (multiply, screen, overlay, darken, lighten, difference), Swipe (the layer shows only left of a divider you slide, to compare it with what's beneath), Masking and Rotation.

items.title: Graphics
items.text: Edit › Graphics draws shapes in a graphics layer (Home › Add Data › Graphics Layer, or one is made with the first graphic). Point, Line, Curve and Polygon are clicked vertex by vertex (double-click to finish); Freehand, Lasso, Rectangle, Circle and Ellipse are dragged. Text places a label where you click, and Dynamic Text adds tokens that update as the map changes: {map}, {scale}, {date}, {time}, {crs}, {layers} and {center}. Picture: drag a rectangle, then pick a PNG or JPEG image to stretch over it. Tools return to Explore after each graphic unless Keep Tool is on. Each graphic keeps its own fill, outline, width and text size in the layer's attributes, so you can edit them in the attribute table or with graphics.style.

items.title: Supported Data Formats
items.text:
This page lists the data formats RustGIS reads and writes, how to add each one, and the main limits. Data covers adding data, large files and rasters in more detail; Maps and Basemaps covers web tile layers.

Most formats open in the desktop app and in the web app alike. Those that need C libraries (GDAL, DuckDB) or files on disk are desktop-only, as the tables say. The web app reads GeoPackages without SQLite, with a small SQLite file reader written in Rust.

items.title: Vector and tabular files
items.text:
Format Extensions or source How to add it Notes GeoJSON .geojson, .json Home › Add Data, or drop the file Features with typed attributes; a GeometryCollection keeps its first member. On the desktop, a FeatureCollection larger than 32 MB is read in place, a view at a time, however large; otherwise files up to 256 MB load whole. Delimited text .csv, .tsv, .txt Add Data, or Add Data › Delimited Text… to choose the columns from the file's header Comma, semicolon, tab or pipe separated (found from the header, or "delimiter"); info.fileColumns lists the columns and the ones found. Points from x/y columns (named like longitude/latitude or easting/northing, or chosen with "x" and "y"), or any geometry from a WKT/EWKT column (named like wkt or geometry, or "wkt"). Coordinates in another system are converted from "crs" (EPSG:2263, or WKT) or an EWKT SRID=; without either, coordinates outside longitude/latitude are pointed out. A file without coordinates opens as a standalone table. Shapefile .shp with .dbf (and .shx), or zipped (.zip) Add Data, drop the file, or upload the zip in the web app A zip may hold several Shapefiles, in folders, and other vector files (GeoJSON, CSV, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf); each becomes a layer, at most 32 for the whole archive (Shapefiles first, so other files are left out when Shapefiles fill it). .txt files and macOS __MACOSX entries are passed over, and a member that can't be read is skipped and named in a notice. Converted to longitude/latitude from the coordinate system in its .prj (EPSG, Esri or OGC WKT; Web Mercator, UTM, State Plane and other common projections); without a .prj it must be in longitude/latitude. On the desktop, one with more than 100,000 shapes (counted from its .shx) is read in place, a view at a time. KML / KMZ .kml, .kmz Add Data, drop the file, or upload it in the web app A layer for each kind of geometry (points, lines, polygons), with each placemark's name, description, folder path and extended data. Styles are kept: the layer is drawn by unique values of its style field, with each KML style's line and fill colours, widths and icon colours (up to 64 styles). Multi-geometries and gx:Tracks are read. Ground overlays (pictures on a LatLonBox, turned by its rotation) are raster layers kept in the project: the picture inside a KMZ, or a file beside a KML (not a web address, nor outside its folder); a gx:LatLonQuad isn't drawn. GPX .gpx Add Data, drop the file, or upload it in the web app Waypoints, routes, tracks (one line per track, its segments as parts) and track points (with elevation and time) as separate layers. Spreadsheets .xlsx, .xlsm, .xlsb, .xls, .ods Add Data (or Delimited Text… to choose the columns), drop the file, or upload it in the web app One sheet at a time, read like delimited text: the first non-empty row names the columns, and x/y or WKT columns (found, or given with "x", "y", "wkt" and "crs") make the geometry; a sheet without them is a table. The first sheet is added and the others named in a notice; "layer" picks one, and info.fileLayers lists them. Dates read as ISO 8601. GeoRSS .rss, .atom, .georss, or .xml Add Data, drop the file, upload, or From URL… RSS 2.0, RSS 1.0 and Atom feeds with GeoRSS Simple, GeoRSS GML or W3C Basic Geo places: points, lines and polygons layers with each item's title, link, description, date, id and category. LandXML .landxml, or .xml Add Data, drop the file, or upload Coordinate geometry points, parcels (polygons), alignments (lines; curves as chords) and TIN surfaces (a triangle per face, with its mean elevation), converted from the file's epsgCode or "crs". Encoded polylines text layer.addEncodedPolyline with "polyline" (one or a list) Google's encoding, precision 5, or 6 ("precision") as OSRM and Valhalla can give: a line layer. GML .gml Add Data, drop the file, or upload Simple features in GML 2 and 3 (WFS answers, OGR's GML): a layer per feature type, its simple elements as fields. Converted from the srsName (EPSG codes, URNs and URLs; the URN and URL forms of geographic systems are latitude first). MapInfo Interchange .mif with its .mid (or both zipped) Add Data, drop the file, or upload the zip Points, lines, polylines, regions (holes found by nesting), rectangles and ellipses; text and arcs are rows without geometry. Converted from the CoordSys: longitude/latitude, Transverse Mercator, Lambert Conformal Conic, Albers or Mercator. OpenStreetMap PBF .osm.pbf Add Data, drop the file, or upload Points (tagged nodes), lines and multipolygons (closed ways that are areas, and multipolygon and boundary relations), with common tags as fields and the rest in other_tags, as GDAL gives them. Up to 40 million nodes (4 million in the web app); on the desktop, extracts over 256 MB open through GDAL when it is installed. TopoJSON .topojson, or .json Add Data, drop the file, or upload A layer per object, its geometries rebuilt from the shared arcs (quantized or not). AutoCAD DXF .dxf (ASCII) Add Data, drop the file, or upload Points, lines and polygons layers from the drawing's entities: POINT, LINE, LWPOLYLINE and POLYLINE (bulges drawn as arcs; closed ones stay lines; polyface meshes become polygons), CIRCLE, ARC, ELLIPSE, SPLINE, HELIX, LEADER, MLINE (its centre line), TEXT, MTEXT, ATTRIB and constant ATTDEF (points with their text, at the alignment point of justified text), HATCH boundaries (holes found by nesting), SOLID, TRACE and 3DFACE (polygons). Blocks (named in any case) are drawn where INSERTs place them (scaled, rotated, in arrays, nested up to 8 deep), and so are DIMENSIONs' blocks (a linear dimension without one draws its lines and measured text). Entities in an object's own coordinate system are turned into the drawing's. Fields: layer, entity, color (ACI, BYLAYER and BYBLOCK resolved), linetype, text, height, rotation, block, elevation and paperspace. The drawing's layouts (paper space: title blocks, viewport frames) are left out, with a notice, unless "paperSpace": true. A drawing never says its coordinate system: give "crs" (such as EPSG:2263), or its coordinates are kept as they are, with a notice. "layer" picks one of the drawing's own layers, and info.fileLayers lists them. Up to 2 million features (500,000 in the web app). Not read: binary DXF, MULTILEADER, WIPEOUT, IMAGE and ACIS solids (3DSOLID, REGION), named in a notice. Geotagged photos .jpg, .jpeg Add Data (several at once in the web app), drop them, upload, or layer.addPhotos with "paths" or a "folder" JPEGs with a GPS position in their EXIF become points in the Photos layer (photos added one at a time join it): each with its name, file, time (when it was taken), altitude, direction (where the camera faced), camera and a thumbnail of at most 160 pixels, kept with the feature so the project needs no other file. Identify shows the thumbnail. Photos without a position are named in a notice and left out; a layer holds up to 2,000 photos. LiDAR point clouds .las, .laz (COPC too) Add Data, drop the file, upload, or From URL… LAS 1.0–1.4 (point formats 0–10) and LAZ, on the desktop and in the web app: a point layer with each point's z, intensity, classification, return and colour (red, green, blue), coloured by ASPRS class (or by elevation when the cloud has one class). A cloud past 2 million points (500,000 in the web app) shows an evenly spread sample of them. Converted from the coordinate system its WKT or GeoTIFF-key record names (the horizontal part of a compound one); a file that names none keeps its coordinates, with a notice. Read in place, so a project keeps the file's path, not its points. GeoPackage .gpkg Add Data, or upload in the web app Every feature table becomes a layer, up to 32 at once (the result counts the rest in skippedCount and names up to 100 of them in skipped); "layer" picks one, and info.fileLayers lists them all. Read in place by its R-tree; any EPSG system is reprojected. The web app reads the file with its own SQLite reader (tables scanned, the envelope in each geometry header tested first; no R-tree); UTF-16 databases aren't read there. GeoParquet .parquet, .geoparquet Add Data, or upload in the web app WKB geometry, with the CRS from the file's geo metadata. Row groups are pruned by the bbox covering. Snappy, gzip, LZ4 and zstd compression are read, in the browser too; Brotli isn't. FlatGeobuf .fgb Add Data, or upload Read in place by its packed R-tree. Standalone tables CSV, or any layer without geometry Add Data Listed under the map in Layers; join or relate them to layers.

Files with more than 100,000 features (GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, and Shapefile on the desktop) are read in place, a view at a time, rather than loaded whole: see Large files. They draw, label, identify and run through tools like any layer; Load All Features loads one to edit it.

items.title: Formats read through GDAL
items.text:
With GDAL installed (its ogr2ogr and ogrinfo on the PATH, GDAL 3.7 or later), the desktop app also reads the vector formats below. Each layer is converted once into a cached, indexed FlatGeobuf, so large ones stream too: see Formats through GDAL.

Format Extensions or source Notes Esri File Geodatabase .gdb folder Every feature class becomes a layer. AutoCAD DWG .dwg Through GDAL's CAD driver, when it is built in. Give "crs" (such as EPSG:2263) when the drawing doesn't say its coordinate system. MapInfo tables .tab Keep the companion files together. OpenStreetMap XML .osm GeoJSON Lines, GMT .geojsonl, .geojsons, .gmt

items.title: Files on the web
items.text:
Home › Add Data › From URL… (layer.addUrl with "url") downloads a file by its https:// (or s3://, see S3 buckets) address and adds it like a file from this computer: GeoJSON, CSV, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, GeoPackage, zipped Shapefiles, KML/KMZ, GPX or GeoTIFF/COG, up to 512 MB on the desktop and 256 MB in the web app (where the server must allow requests from web pages, CORS). The format comes from the address, or from the contents when the address has no extension (an API endpoint, say). The app downloads in the background and adds the layer when the file arrives (to the project it was started in: opening another meanwhile drops it). A .pmtiles address is added as a tile layer and read a tile at a time instead.

A cloud-optimised GeoTIFF (a tiled .tif with overviews, as most published imagery is) is read in place rather than downloaded: its header first, then, by HTTP range requests, only the tiles of the overview each part of the view needs, so a Sentinel-2 scene of 300 MB draws in a couple of seconds and full detail comes as you zoom in. It is a tile layer (map.addTiles kind cog, saved in the project by its address), drawn under the map's own layers like other tile layers: RGB(A) 8-bit images as they are, other images in grey stretched between the 2nd and 98th percentiles of their coarsest overview. A GeoTIFF in strips, with bands stored apart, or without tiles is downloaded whole as a raster layer, as is any GeoTIFF added with "whole": true (for the raster tools and symbology). The web app needs the server to allow range requests from web pages (CORS with the Range header), as public buckets such as Sentinel-2's do.

A GeoParquet or FlatGeobuf file by its address is read in place too, a view at a time, however large: the layer is streamed like a large local file, and the view's features are fetched in the background by HTTP range requests and drawn as they land. A FlatGeobuf's header and packed R-tree index are read first (a level of the tree per round of requests), then only the features in the view. A GeoParquet's footer is read first, then the row groups the view meets, by their bounding box covering column (bbox) and its statistics: the covering of groups on the view's edge, then the geometry and attribute columns of the rows taken. A view holding more than a read takes (60,000 features on the desktop, 30,000 in the web app) shows an evenly spread sample of it, in patches; zoom in for all of them. So a 12 GB FlatGeobuf of 11 million areas opens after 65 KB and draws a city in about a second from 9 MB, and a 525 MB Overture buildings file opens after 1 MB. The project keeps the address and reads it the same way when it opens. A FlatGeobuf without an index, a GeoParquet without a covering column, or a server that doesn't answer range requests means the file is downloaded whole instead, as is any file added with "whole": true; Load All Features and the geoprocessing tools fetch the whole file on the desktop, while in the web app they need the file downloaded first.

layer.addUrl waits for the download, up to a minute, which suits the command line, MCP and the desktop app's assistant; a larger file comes through the From URL… dialog, which downloads in the background. In the web app, where nothing may wait, it adds .pmtiles and GeoTIFF addresses only (a GeoTIFF read in place); other files, GeoParquet and FlatGeobuf read in place among them, come through the From URL… dialog (ui.addUrl) or a ?data= link. GeoJSON, CSV, KML and GPX files are read up to 256 MB; larger downloads (GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, GeoPackage, GeoTIFF) up to the limits above.

items.title: Map and feature services
items.text:
Home › Add Data › From Service… connects to a service by its address, lists what it offers from its capabilities. For OGC API feature collections, enter a group name (initially My OGC Layer) and choose Import All. The group expands into ordinary point, line and polygon layers with the same legends, styling and attribute tables as file imports. Other offerings have individual Add buttons (service.layers and service.add from scripts, the command line and MCP). An OGC API landing page works directly: RustGIS follows its advertised JSON collections link, so you don't need to append /collections. If the landing page also offers map tiles, they remain listed alongside the collections. A failed collections request leaves any available map layers usable and shows the error.

Right-click the group and choose Refresh to rediscover its collections and update them all, including newly added or removed collections. Right-click a child and choose Refresh to update only that collection. Existing children keep their names, styles and visibility (a changed geometry type gets a suitable default symbol); selections are cleared because row positions can change. Refresh replaces local feature edits with the service's data. Failed imports or refreshes leave the map intact; a successful operation is one undo step. Groups and their source connections are saved in the project. Group downloads are limited to 2000 collections and 64 MB in total and use the existing per-collection feature limits.

Scripts use service.import {"url":"…","name":"My OGC Layer"} and service.refresh {"group":id} or service.refresh {"layer":id}. The browser uses service.groupPlan to discover the requests, then supplies text, documents, and responses: [{"url":"…","text":"GeoJSON"}] to import or refresh without blocking network calls.

Service What it lists How a layer is added WMS 1.1.1 / 1.3.0 Named layers offered in Web Mercator A tile layer of GetMap images (PNG when the service offers it, else JPEG) WMTS Layers whose tile matrix set is Web Mercator's pyramid A tile layer from the tile template (or KVP GetTile) WFS 1.1 / 2.0 Feature types Their features downloaded as GeoJSON, in the output format the service names (up to 50,000) OGC API Features Collections Their items downloaded as GeoJSON OGC API Tiles Collections' map and vector tiles; a landing page's dataset map tiles A tile layer in WebMercatorQuad, from the tile template the tileset advertises (its item link; …/tiles/WebMercatorQuad/{z}/{y}/{x}, the usual path, when that can't be read), keeping the tiles link's query (a token), map tiles in the server's image format, vector tiles drawn layer by layer in colours of their own WCS 1.0 / 2.0 (a 1.1 service is asked in 1.0) Coverages, with their bounds A raster: GetCoverage of the map's view within the coverage's bounds (or its whole extent: "bbox": "full"), as a GeoTIFF in EPSG:4326, at most 2048 pixels on a side ArcGIS REST FeatureServer and MapServer layers; a MapServer's map; an ImageServer; a VectorTileServer Layers queried as GeoJSON (up to the server's record limit); a map as its tile cache when it is Web Mercator's pyramid, else exported images; an ImageServer as exported images; a VectorTileServer as its MapLibre style

The type is guessed from the address (?SERVICE=, /wmts, /wfs, /wcs, /collections, /rest/services…) or chosen (select OGC API Features and Tiles when a landing page's address doesn't identify its type). A WebMercatorQuad tileset is found by its tile matrix set, whatever the server calls it. A service that asks for a token says so. In the web app the server must allow requests from web pages (CORS).

A coverage is read once, for the view when it was added (its DescribeCoverage first, for its axes, format and bounds; service.coverage gives the GetCoverage address alone). Moving the map doesn't ask for it again: add it again for another area. The server reprojects it to EPSG:4326 (WCS 2.0 through its CRS extension); one that can't answers with an error, which is shown.

For callers that fetch documents themselves (including the web app), service.layers accepts text for the initial document and documents: [{"url": "…", "text": "…"}] for subsequent responses. It returns next while another collections document is needed; supplied documents never cause a blocking capabilities fetch. Each listed layer includes source_url; pass it and the same documents to service.add to distinguish layers with the same name. Discovery follows at most four documents and rejects loops and disallowed addresses. Feature downloads retain their existing limits; this does not add collection-list or feature pagination.

items.title: Catalogues
items.text: The same dialog's Catalogue search (CSW) type searches a CSW 2.0.2 catalogue (GeoNetwork, pycsw, geocat.ch…) by words anywhere in its records and, if you like, the map's area (catalog.search). Its records are listed 20 at a time (More asks for the next), with their titles, abstracts (on hover) and bounds (Zoom), and a button per link RustGIS can follow: a WMS, WMTS, WFS, WCS, OGC API or ArcGIS service connects in the dialog, a download is added as From URL… does. Links pointing where a document on the web may not send RustGIS (the local network) are left out.

items.title: PostgreSQL and PostGIS
items.text:
The desktop app reads the geometry and geography columns of a PostGIS database live, talking to the server itself: see PostgreSQL and PostGIS.

Source How to add it Notes PostGIS table or view Add Data › Database… (layer.addDatabase) with a libpq connection string or postgresql:// address Large tables read a view at a time by their spatial index, others loaded whole. Converted to longitude/latitude by the server; "crs" for geometry that doesn't say. A column of mixed types becomes a layer per type. The password is kept for the session only.

items.title: SQL queries and DuckDB databases
items.text:
With DuckDB installed (the duckdb program on the PATH, DuckDB 1.5 or later), the desktop app adds the result of an SQL query as a layer, and opens DuckDB database files. Results are written as cached GeoParquet, so large ones stream too: see SQL queries and DuckDB databases.

Source How to add it Notes SQL query layer.addSql with "sql" One DuckDB SELECT with DuckDB Spatial: Parquet, CSV, GeoParquet and ST_Read files, web addresses (https://, s3://). Give "crs" for a geometry that doesn't say its coordinate system. DuckDB database .duckdb, .ddb: Add Data Every table with a geometry column becomes a layer ("layer" picks one). Converted once, until the file changes.

items.title: Rasters
items.text: Format Extensions or source How to add it Notes GeoTIFF / Cloud-optimised GeoTIFF .tif, .tiff Add Data, or upload Regular or cloud-optimised, striped or tiled; grey, RGB(A), palette (with its colour table) or multiband; Deflate, LZW, PackBits, JPEG or Zstandard compression. Any EPSG system, or the file's own projection from its GeoKeys (Albers, LCC, transverse Mercator…), reprojected as it draws. A large file opens from its overview, or one made as it is read when it has none. ASCII grid .asc (with an optional .prj) Add Data, or upload Zarr a store's folder (.zarr) or web address, format 2 (consolidated) or 3 Add Data › Zarr… (layer.addZarr), Add Data on the folder, or a ?zarr= link A variable's latitude/longitude (or y/x) map at the steps picked of its other dimensions (time, level), read chunk by chunk in pure Rust (blosc, zlib, gzip, zstd, LZ4; sharded arrays too), on the desktop and the web. See Zarr stores. Rasters GDAL reads .jp2, .img, .hgt, .dem, .dt0–.dt2, .nc, .hdf, .h5, .bil, .grd, .sdat, .kea, .ers, .rst, .ntf, .ecw, .sid… Add Data (desktop, with GDAL installed: gdal_translate, gdalinfo and gdalwarp) Converted once to a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF in the cache, then read as one. A NetCDF or HDF file's variables are its subdatasets: the first is added, the others are named in a notice, and "layer" picks one. A file that doesn't say its coordinate system is read as WGS 84 when its coordinates look like longitude/latitude (0–360° longitudes are moved to -180–180°); otherwise give "crs".

items.title: Tiles and web services
items.text: Format Extensions or source How to add it Notes Raster tiles XYZ/TMS template ({z}/{x}/{y}, {-y}, {s}, {q}), WMS ({bbox-epsg-3857}) Home › Add › Basemap › Add Tile Layer PNG, JPEG and WebP. Vector tiles Mapbox Vector Tiles (.pbf, .mvt) template, or TileJSON Add Tile Layer Drawn in a built-in style that knows the OpenMapTiles, Protomaps and Shortbread schemas. MapLibre styles style.json Add Tile Layer The style's vector and raster sources, sprite, expressions and zoom functions. PMTiles .pmtiles: a web address, or a file on the desktop Add Tile Layer (or its Tile Archive File… button), Add Data, or drop the file Raster or vector, as the archive says. Read a tile at a time by byte ranges (the server must allow them, and CORS in the web app). A vector archive is drawn in the built-in style when it is a basemap, otherwise with each of its layers in its own colour. MBTiles .mbtiles: a file Add Data, drop the file, Add Tile Layer's Tile Archive File… button, or upload in the web app Raster (PNG, JPEG, WebP) or vector tiles, as its metadata says, drawn as PMTiles archives are. The desktop reads the file in place, a tile at a time. The web app reads an upload into memory (the plain tiles table and the deduplicated layouts of mbutil, TileMill and Planetiler) and keeps it for the session: a project saved there asks for the file again.

items.title: Writing
items.text: Format How to write it Notes GeoJSON, CSV Data › Export (share.exportLayer) The Export Features dialog picks the format; the file is saved in it whatever extension is typed. In the web app it downloads (any format below but GeoPackage; a Shapefile as one zip). A streamed layer writes its whole source (as every format below does). GeoPackage Data › Export to .gpkg (desktop) One feature table (an attributes table for a layer without geometry) in WGS 84, with an R-tree spatial index and the GeoPackage 1.4 triggers that keep it current when other software edits the file. Feature ids are kept. GeoParquet Data › Export to .parquet GeoParquet 1.1: WKB geometry in WGS 84, Snappy compression, row groups of 65,536 features and a bbox covering column so readers can skip rows by extent. Shapefile Data › Export to .shp (or .zip for the files zipped) Writes .shp, .shx, .dbf, .prj (WGS 84) and .cpg (UTF-8). Field names are cut to 10 characters (made unique), text to 254 bytes, and numbers too wide for a dBase field are left empty; features without geometry, and lines of a single point, are left out (and reported). FlatGeobuf Data › Export to .fgb With a spatial index; features without geometry are left out (and reported). KML, KMZ, GPX Data › Export to .kml, .kmz or .gpx Placemarks named by a name field, if there is one; features without geometry are left out. KML, GPX, CSV with WKT Analyze › Workflows › Data Interop GeoTIFF Data › Export PNG Publish › Export Map (share.exportMap) At any DPI, with labels, scale bar and tile credits. PDF Layouts, reports and presentations Wavefront OBJ, glTF Publish › Export To 3D, Share As › Web Scene Polygons extruded by a field. Web map, OGC API Features, MapLibre style Publish › Share As Open-format files that need no server: see Sharing. Raster tiles Analyze › Create Hosted Imagery

items.title: RustGIS files
items.text: File Extension Notes Project .rgis (older .rgisx open too) Saves streamed layers' file paths, not their features; a browser upload is kept inside. Map, layer, style, color ramp, template, task, bookmark and layout files .rgismap, .rgislyr, .rgisstyle, .rgisramp, .rgistemplate, .rgistask, .rgisbookmarks, .rgislayout See Project items. Project package .rgispkg Everything, rasters included. Plugin .rgplugin See Plugins. Color ramps from other tools QGIS style .xml and layer style .qml, GDAL color-relief .txt, GMT .cpt Read as custom color ramps; see Custom color ramps.

items.title: Formats
items.text:
Every format, with how to add it and its limits, is listed on Supported Data Formats.
