Format Read Write GeoJSON (.geojson, .json) Yes Yes Delimited text (.csv, .tsv, .txt) with x/y columns in any coordinate system, or WKT geometry Yes Yes Shapefile (.shp + .dbf, or zipped in a .zip) Yes (the web app opens zips) Yes (share.exportLayer) GeoPackage (.gpkg, every feature table) Yes Yes (desktop) GeoParquet (.parquet, .geoparquet, WKB geometry) Yes Yes FlatGeobuf (.fgb) Yes Yes (share.exportLayer) KML/KMZ (with their styles), GPX Yes Yes Spreadsheets (.xlsx, .xls, .ods), GeoRSS feeds, LandXML, encoded polylines Yes No GML, MapInfo MIF/MID, OpenStreetMap PBF, TopoJSON, AutoCAD DXF (ASCII) Yes No LiDAR point clouds: LAS, LAZ, COPC (an evenly spread sample) Yes No Geotagged photos (JPEG with EXIF GPS): points with their thumbnails Yes No Through GDAL: File Geodatabase (.gdb folder), AutoCAD DWG, MapInfo TAB, OpenStreetMap XML… Yes (desktop, when GDAL is installed) No PostgreSQL/PostGIS databases, read live (large tables a view at a time) Yes (desktop) No DuckDB databases (.duckdb, .ddb) and SQL queries Yes (desktop, when DuckDB is installed) No KML, GPX, CSV with WKT geometry No Yes (Analyze › Workflows › Data Interop) GeoTIFF and cloud-optimised GeoTIFF (.tif, .tiff) Yes Yes ASCII grid (.asc, with an optional .prj) Yes No Through GDAL: JPEG 2000, ERDAS Imagine, SRTM HGT, DTED, NetCDF, HDF, ENVI, SAGA… Yes (desktop, when GDAL is installed) No Web tiles: XYZ/TMS/WMS rasters, Mapbox Vector Tiles, MapLibre styles, PMTiles and MBTiles archives Yes Yes (Analyze › Create Hosted Imagery) RustGIS project (.rgis; older .rgisx files open too) Yes Yes

Add data with Home › Add Data (From URL… adds a file by its web address, reading a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF, GeoParquet or FlatGeobuf in place, a view at a time, and downloading others; see Files on the web), by dropping files on the window, or by passing them on the command line (rustgis places.geojson). Home › Add Data › Delimited Text… asks for a CSV or a spreadsheet first, then lists its columns to pick the x and y (or WKT) ones from, with the coordinate system (such as EPSG:2263) and the separator (changing it reads the columns again); info.fileColumns lists them for scripts. Add Data finds them itself (columns named like longitude/latitude, easting/northing or geometry, and EWKT's SRID=) and says when coordinates aren't longitude/latitude. A CSV without coordinate columns, or a layer without geometry, opens as a standalone table, listed under the map in Layers; right-click it to open or remove it. Tables can share a name: commands and tools take a table's id (info.project lists them) as well as its name, which stands for the first table of that name. An id given as a number is never taken for a name. The Tools pane and Geocode Addresses send the id of the table picked; a tool's run keeps the table's name beside it (input_name). The XY Table To Point tool (Geoprocessing, and a table's right-click menu) makes points of a table already in the project, from two fields of coordinates and their coordinate system. In a text field a single comma is the decimal separator (1,234 is 1.234); thousands separators are not read. Home › Add Data › Graphics Layer adds a layer for drawn graphics, and Insert › Layer Templates adds empty layers with ready-made schemas to draw into.

Vector coordinates are WGS 84 longitude/latitude and are displayed in Web Mercator. GeoPackage, GeoParquet and FlatGeobuf files in another coordinate system (any EPSG code) are converted as they are read. Rasters keep their own coordinate system (any EPSG code, such as UTM zones or national grids) and are reprojected on the fly as they draw.

items.title: Formats through GDAL
items.text: When GDAL is installed (its ogr2ogr and ogrinfo programs on the PATH, or the folder holding them in RUSTGIS_GDAL_BIN; GDAL 3.7 or later), the desktop app also opens the vector formats GDAL reads: File Geodatabases, DWG, MapInfo TAB, OpenStreetMap XML and more. RustGIS doesn't link to GDAL: each layer is converted once, by ogr2ogr, into a FlatGeobuf with a spatial index in WGS 84 (GDAL reprojects it), kept in the cache folder (~/.cache/rustgis/gdal on Linux, ~/Library/Caches/RustGIS/gdal on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\RustGIS\cache\gdal on Windows, or RUSTGIS_GDAL_CACHE). Adding the file again reuses the conversion until the file changes, and large layers stream like any large FlatGeobuf (below). Every layer of the file is added; a layer mixing geometry types is added as one layer per type. Projects remember the original file and convert it again if the cached copy is gone.

items.title: SQL queries and DuckDB databases
items.text:
When DuckDB is installed (the duckdb program on the PATH, or the folder holding it in RUSTGIS_DUCKDB_BIN; DuckDB 1.5 or later), the desktop app adds the result of an SQL query as a layer, with the layer.addSql command (Add Data From SQL in command search):

{"sql": "SELECT name, geometry FROM read_parquet('places.parquet') WHERE country = 'FR'", "name": "French places"}

Analyze › SQL opens the SQL pane, a workspace for these queries: an editor (Ctrl+Enter runs the query) that completes table and column names of the database named above it and DuckDB Spatial's common functions, the result's first 200 rows as a table, Add to Map for a result with a geometry column, and a history of the queries run (kept by the app with its preferences, without the database's password; a query that seems to hold a credential, such as user:password@ in an address, a signed URL or a secret, isn't kept). Queries run in the background, so the app keeps drawing while DuckDB works. The commands behind it are sql.query (a query's first rows, up to 1,000, without adding a layer) and sql.schema (a database's tables and their columns); both take "database" as layer.addSql does. The web app has no DuckDB, so the pane says to open the project in the desktop app.

The query is one DuckDB SELECT (or FROM …, WITH …), with DuckDB Spatial's ST_ functions: it can read Parquet, CSV, JSON and GeoParquet files, anything ST_Read reads, and web addresses (https://, s3://), so a bounding box of Overture Maps is one query:

SELECT id, names.primary AS name, geometry
FROM read_parquet('s3://overturemaps-us-west-2/release/2026-09-23.1/theme=places/type=place/*', hive_partitioning = 1)
WHERE bbox.xmin BETWEEN -83.95 AND -83.89 AND bbox.ymin BETWEEN 35.94 AND 35.98

The first geometry column becomes the layer's geometry; other columns become its attributes (types RustGIS doesn't read, such as dates and lists, as text). A geometry that says its coordinate system is converted to longitude/latitude; give "crs" (such as EPSG:2263) for one that doesn't. A result mixing geometry types becomes a layer per type, and rows without a geometry are left out. "database" opens a DuckDB database (read only) so the query names its tables plainly; the database is trusted like the query, since its views run as part of it.

Home › Add Data opens a DuckDB database file (.duckdb, .ddb): every table with a geometry column becomes a layer ("layer" picks one).

items.title: PostgreSQL and PostGIS
items.text:
Home › Add Data › Database… (layer.addDatabase) connects to a PostgreSQL database with PostGIS and reads its tables live. RustGIS talks to the server itself (nothing else to install; TLS as libpq does it). sslmode=prefer (the default) and require encrypt the connection but don't check the server's certificate, so they don't protect against a server in the middle: use verify-full (or verify-ca, which here checks the host name too) on networks you don't trust. The certificate is checked against sslrootcert (a private authority's PEM file) or the web's roots. disable turns TLS off. The connection is a libpq connection string (host=localhost port=5432 dbname=gis user=postgres) or a postgresql://user@host/dbname address; what it leaves out comes from PGHOST, PGPORT, PGUSER and PGDATABASE, as with libpq. List Tables (info.databaseTables) shows the tables and views with a geometry or geography column, and every one of them becomes a layer unless one is chosen (table, schema.table, or table:column for one of several geometry columns). The connection is read only.

A table of more than 100,000 rows (or any, with "stream": true) is read in place a view at a time, like a large GeoParquet: the view's box is matched against the column's spatial index, and when more rows match than a view draws, an evenly spread sample of them is numbered on the server, so only those cross the network. Smaller tables are loaded whole, so they can be edited. The server converts geometry to longitude/latitude (ST_Transform, so every coordinate system in its spatial_ref_sys works) and curves to lines; give "crs" (such as EPSG:2263) for a column whose geometry doesn't say its coordinate system. A column of mixed geometry types becomes a layer per type, and empty tables (such as the TIGER geocoder's) are left out. Features keep their ids between views: the table's integer primary key, else the row's place in the table (the rows of a view or a partitioned table without a key are numbered as read, so theirs can change between views).

The password is kept until RustGIS closes and never written to the project, which names the connection without it. Without one, PGPASSWORD or libpq's password file (~/.pgpass, or %APPDATA%\postgresql\pgpass.conf) serve when you add a table. A project keeps a streamed table's connection and reads it again when it opens, sending only a password given in this session: a project file could name any host, and must never get your own credentials. When the server wants a password, connect again with Add Data › Database… (the layer reads again when the project is next opened). A small table's features are kept in the project as they were when added.

layer.addSql takes a connection as its "database" too, through DuckDB's postgres extension (installed the first time, like DuckDB Spatial), so a query names its tables plainly; the password reaches DuckDB in its environment (PGPASSWORD), never on its command line:

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'layer.addSql={"sql":"SELECT name, geom FROM roads WHERE lanes > 2","database":"postgres:host=localhost dbname=gis user=postgres","password":"…"}'

RustGIS doesn't link to DuckDB: it runs duckdb, which writes the result as GeoParquet in the cache folder (~/.cache/rustgis/duckdb on Linux, ~/Library/Caches/RustGIS/duckdb on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\RustGIS\cache\duckdb on Windows, or RUSTGIS_DUCKDB_CACHE), sorted along a Hilbert curve with a bounding-box covering, so large results stream like any large GeoParquet (below). DuckDB Spatial is installed the first time (a download from DuckDB's extension repository). A database table is converted once and reused until the file changes; a query runs afresh each time. Projects convert a table again if the cached result is gone, but never run a query when they open: run it again. A database is read on its own, shut out of other files and web addresses, so a view in it that reaches elsewhere fails rather than reading them.

A query can read any file the app can and fetch any web address, and a database is a file or a server, so the AI Assistant asks before it runs a query or reads a database, and plugins need both the files and network permissions.

items.title: STAC catalogs
items.text:
Home › Add Data › STAC Search… searches a STAC API for imagery and other assets: by collection, dates, the most cloud cover and (by default) where the map is. The default API is Element 84's Earth Search (Sentinel-2, Landsat, NAIP, Copernicus DEM and Sentinel-1 on AWS); Microsoft's Planetary Computer is offered beside it, and any STAC API with item search works. Collections lists what the API offers, Find Items shows up to 50 items (date, cloud cover, id) and draws their footprints as a layer; a click frames an item, and Add adds the asset chosen beside it: visual (true colour) when there is one, else the first GeoTIFF, else the first data asset. A cloud-optimised GeoTIFF is read in place, the tiles each view needs by range (see Files on the web); other assets download whole.

The commands do the same: stac.collections ("url"), stac.search ("collections", "bbox" as [west, south, east, north] or "view", "datetime" such as 2024-06-01/2024-06-30, "limit", "maxCloud", "footprints"), and stac.addAsset with an item stac.search returned ("item") or an item's address ("url") and "asset":

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'stac.search={"collections":"sentinel-2-l2a","bbox":[7.4,46.9,7.5,47],"datetime":"2024-07-01/2024-07-31","maxCloud":20}' --cmd 'stac.addAsset={"url":"https://earth-search.aws.element84.com/v1/collections/sentinel-2-l2a/items/S2B_32TLS_20240727_0_L2A","asset":"scl"}'

Assets are added by their web address: one in a cloud store's own protocol (s3://) is refused with a message saying so, and an item on the web can't point into the local network. A Planetary Computer asset (in Azure Blob Storage) is signed first: RustGIS asks the Planetary Computer's token service for its storage container's token and reuses it for half an hour. The token is part of the layer's address, so a project saved with one reads it again only while the token lasts (about an hour): add the asset again after that. A ?stac= link opens the web app on an item or a collection (web app links). Searches reach the network, so the AI Assistant asks before it runs them, and plugins need the network permission.

items.title: Overture Maps
items.text:
Home › Add Data › Overture Maps… adds Overture Maps' open data: buildings, places, transportation (segments and connectors), administrative divisions, base layers (land use, land, land cover, water, infrastructure, bathymetry) and addresses, from the latest release (or one named with "release"). Two ways:

  • The features where the map is. A theme's type is a few hundred GeoParquet files, each covering an area; Overture's STAC catalog gives every file's extent, so only the files that cover the map's view are read, in place by range like any GeoParquet by address (see Files on the web), and each becomes a layer read a view at a time. Zoom to a city or smaller: a view that takes more than six files is refused (a country takes dozens).
  • Map tiles of the whole world, from the theme's PMTiles archive: every zoom, drawn a layer per type. Some themes' tiles hold their features only when zoomed in (places from zoom 14).

overture.add does the same ("theme", "type", "bbox" or the view, "tiles": true for the tiles):

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'map.zoomToExtent={"extent":[7.40,46.93,7.47,46.97]}' --cmd 'overture.add={"theme":"buildings"}' --cmd 'overture.add={"theme":"transportation"}' --cmd 'share.exportMap={"path":"bern.png"}'

The data's licences differ by theme (OpenStreetMap's ODbL for most, CDLA Permissive 2.0 for places); the layer says which.

items.title: Source Cooperative
items.text: Home › Add Data › Source Cooperative… lists Source Cooperative's featured products (or an account's), browses a product's folders and adds a file by its address on the data proxy (https://data.source.coop/<account>/<product>/…): GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs and PMTiles are read in place, other files downloaded. sourcecoop.products ("account") and sourcecoop.list ("account", "product", "path") list them; a listed file's "url" is added with layer.addUrl. Like STAC searches, these reach the network: the AI Assistant asks first and plugins need the network permission.

items.title: Geocoding addresses
items.text:
Home › Add Data › Geocode Addresses… (layer.geocode) turns a table's addresses into points: a CSV of addresses without coordinates is added as a standalone table, then each row's address fields ("address": a field, or several such as street, city and country, joined with commas) are looked up, each distinct address once. The result is a new point layer holding every field plus geocoded, what the geocoder called the place; rows that weren't found stay in its table without a point.

The geocoder is OpenStreetMap's public Nominatim by default, or Photon ("provider": "photon"). Their usage policies allow light use, so RustGIS sends them at most one request a second and 100 addresses a run; give "url" of a Nominatim or Photon server of your own for more (up to 10,000, with no wait between requests). In the app the requests go out in the background, one at a time, and the layer is added when the last answer lands; layer.geocode on the command line waits for them.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'layer.addData={"path":"stores.csv"}' --cmd 'layer.geocode={"table":"stores","address":["street","city","country"]}'

The addresses are sent to the geocoder's server, so the AI Assistant asks before it geocodes, and plugins need the network permission.

items.title: OpenStreetMap and administrative boundaries
items.text:
Home › Add Data › OpenStreetMap… (osm.download) downloads OpenStreetMap data where the map is from an Overpass server: a preset (buildings, roads, railways, water, land use, parks, points of interest or administrative boundaries) or tag filters such as amenity=cafe, shop. The answer becomes up to three layers, points, lines and polygons: closed ways that are areas (buildings, land use and the like, as OSM reads their tags) are polygons, and multipolygon and boundary relations are assembled from their members. A layer's fields are its 25 most common tags, the rest in other_tags as GDAL writes them. The area can be up to 0.25 square degrees (about 50 × 50 km), and an answer up to 50,000 elements: the public servers are shared, so a larger area is better read from an extract (.osm.pbf). "url" names another Overpass server when the public one is busy.

Home › Add Data › Boundaries… (boundaries.add) adds a country's administrative boundaries from geoBoundaries (CC BY 4.0): the country itself (ADM0), its states or provinces (ADM1) and finer divisions down to ADM5 where they exist, simplified for the map. boundaries.countries lists the countries.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'osm.download={"bbox":[7.44,46.944,7.456,46.952],"preset":"buildings"}' --cmd 'boundaries.add={"country":"KEN","level":"ADM1"}'

Both reach the network: the AI Assistant asks before it runs them, and plugins need the network permission. OpenStreetMap data is © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL).

items.title: Open-data portals
items.text:
Home › Add Data › Search Open Data… (portal.search) finds datasets by text in an open-data portal and lists, for each, the resources RustGIS can add, the best format first:

  • data.gov and CKAN catalogues: catalog.data.gov by default, or a CKAN site by its address (https://open.canada.ca/data, https://data.gov.uk…). GeoJSON, FlatGeobuf, GeoParquet, GeoPackage, KML, zipped Shapefiles, GeoTIFF, CSV, WMS, WFS and ArcGIS REST resources are offered; web pages, PDFs and the like are left out.
  • Socrata: every Socrata site through its discovery API, or one site such as data.cityofnewyork.us. Datasets with a location column are added as their GeoJSON export (up to 50,000 rows).
  • ArcGIS Hub: hub.arcgis.com or an organisation's Hub site; its feature services.

Only where the map is keeps to datasets covering the map's view. A file is added by its address (portal.add, read in place when it can be, as Add Data From URL… does); a service opens Add From Service… connected to it, to pick its layer (portal.add takes the first layer with features unless "layer" names one). A search lists up to 50 datasets.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'portal.search={"portal":"socrata","url":"data.cityofnewyork.us","query":"parks"}'
rustgis-cli run --sample --cmd 'portal.add={"url":"https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/enfh-gkve.geojson?$limit=50000","name":"Parks","portal":"https://api.us.socrata.com"}'

An address a portal lists is judged as one found in a document on the web: it may not point into the local network. Both commands reach the network, so the AI Assistant asks before it runs them, and plugins need the network permission. A dataset's licence is the portal's: its page (the Page link) says what it is.

items.title: S3 buckets
items.text:
An s3://bucket/key address works wherever data is added by its address: Add Data › From URL… and layer.addUrl (a cloud-optimised GeoTIFF is read in place by range, other files are downloaded), PMTiles archives, ?data= links, and STAC assets whose address is an s3:// one. A public bucket needs nothing more: it is read anonymously from AWS.

Home › Add Data › S3… (s3.connect) connects to a private bucket, or to an S3-compatible service (MinIO, Cloudflare R2, Wasabi, source.coop…) by its endpoint, and browses a bucket a folder at a time (s3.list), adding an object with Add. A connection names its endpoint (AWS when empty), its region and the buckets it serves: the ones it is given ("buckets") and the ones browsed through it this session. An s3:// address of one of them is read through that connection, signed (AWS Signature Version 4) with its keys; an address of any other bucket (a project's, a link's) is read anonymously from AWS, never with your keys or from your endpoint. Keys are typed, or, on the desktop and only when chosen, read from an AWS profile ("profile": ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.aws/config) or from the environment ("environment": true: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN, AWS_REGION); without any, the connection is anonymous. AWS, anonymous in the dialog browses with no keys at all.

rustgis-cli run --cmd 's3.connect={"name":"minio","endpoint":"https://minio.example.org","buckets":["my-bucket"],"accessKeyId":"…","secretAccessKey":"…"}' \
  --cmd 's3.list={"url":"s3://my-bucket/rasters/"}' --cmd 'layer.addUrl={"url":"s3://my-bucket/rasters/dem.tif"}'

Keys are kept until RustGIS closes: never in a project (which keeps the s3:// address), a command's result, a notice or the log. Remember keeps a connection's name, endpoint and region in the app's settings, never its secret; storing secrets in the system keychain isn't supported. Keys go only to the endpoint they're for: a signed request that is redirected isn't followed, and keys from a profile or the environment are used only with AWS or the profile's own endpoint_url. In the web app, the bucket's CORS rules must allow the page's origin (and, for a private bucket, the Authorization and x-amz-* headers). The AI Assistant asks before it connects or lists; plugins can't connect, and need the network permission to list.

items.title: Data Sources
items.text:
The Data Sources pane (View › Windows › Data Sources, ui.pane.sources) gathers the places data comes from:

  • Favourites: any source, right-clicked and added.
  • Recent: the last 20 sources added (files, web addresses, tile layers, services, database tables, Zarr variables, STAC assets, sample data), newest first.
  • Folders: the folders connected to the Browser (Add Folder…; desktop).
  • Services, Databases (desktop) and STAC APIs: addresses saved with the box under each. A click opens Add From Service, Add From Database or STAC Search connected to it, which lists its layers, tables or collections.
  • S3: this session's connections; a click opens the S3 browser on it.
  • Library: well-known public sources: OpenStreetMap tiles, EOX Sentinel-2 cloudless and NASA GIBS (WMTS), USGS imagery, topographic and hydrography maps (ArcGIS), GEBCO bathymetry (WMS), Earth Search and Planetary Computer (STAC), and the Natural Earth sample layers.

A click on a file, a web address, a tile layer or a sample adds it at once. The lists are kept with the app's preferences, never in a project. They hold no secrets: a web address loses its password and any key, token or signature in its query (token=, sig=, X-Amz-*…), and a database is kept without its password. The commands sources.list, sources.save, sources.favourite and sources.remove read and change the lists, for the command line and the AI Assistant. On the command line they last for the run.

items.title: Large files
items.text:
GeoPackage, GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf and (on the desktop) Shapefile files with more than 100,000 features are read in place rather than loaded whole, so files far larger than memory open in a moment. The layer reads the features in view, using the file's own spatial index (the GeoPackage R-tree, the FlatGeobuf packed R-tree, GeoParquet row-group bounding boxes; for a Shapefile, the shapes' bounding boxes, read once when it opens), in the background as the map moves. When a view holds more than 250,000 features (100,000 in the web app), the layer draws an evenly spread sample of them and its tooltip in Layers says so: zoom in to see them all. Smaller files load whole; layer.addData with "stream": true or false overrides the choice.

On the desktop, a GeoJSON FeatureCollection larger than 32 MB is read the same way, with no size limit: opening reads the file once, keeping each feature's place in it and its bounding box (a file over 256 MB through a buffer, so it is never held whole), and each view parses just the features it shows. A single feature, a bare geometry or TopoJSON is loaded whole.

A streamed layer works like any other for symbology, labels, pop-ups, selection and the attribute table (which lists the features read for the view). Geoprocessing tools read the whole file. Edits are refused, since the features are read again as the view moves: right-click the layer in Layers and choose Load All Features (layer.loadAll) to load it into memory and edit it. Projects save the layer's file path, not its features, and read the file again when they open; a browser upload is kept in the project.

File Features A view read GeoParquet, 0.1° grid (50 MB) 1.6 million polygons 183,000 in 0.15 s FlatGeobuf, the same grid (335 MB) 1.6 million polygons 183,000 in 0.11 s GeoPackage, the same grid (344 MB) 1.6 million polygons 183,000 in 0.18 s GeoParquet, global grid (190 MB) 6.5 million polygons a sample of 136,000 in 0.27 s

items.title: Rasters
items.text:
Add a GeoTIFF or an ASCII grid with Add Data, by dropping it on the window, or in the web app by picking it. An ASCII grid takes its coordinate system from a .prj file next to it (as a Shapefile does); otherwise, and always in the web app, which only sees the one file, it must be in longitude/latitude degrees. Exporting a raster opened from an overview writes that overview. GeoTIFFs may be regular or cloud-optimised: grey, RGB(A), palette (coloured by the file's colour table, as land cover such as the NLCD is) or multiband, of any pixel type, tiled or striped, and compressed with Deflate, LZW, PackBits, JPEG or Zstandard. The coordinate system is an EPSG code, or the file's own projection described in its GeoKeys (Albers, Lambert conformal conic, transverse Mercator, Mercator, Lambert azimuthal, stereographic, equirectangular and others), which an exported GeoTIFF keeps. A raster too large to hold in memory (more than 120 million samples, 32 million in the web app) opens from its largest overview that fits; one without overviews opens as an overview made as it is read, a strip or tile at a time (every second, fourth… pixel each way), so reading it takes as long as decoding the whole file once. A cloud-optimised GeoTIFF added by its web address is read in place instead, a tile at a time (see Files on the web).

The web app opens a picked or dropped file of up to 256 MB whole. A larger GeoTIFF is read a part at a time instead: its header, then only the tiles of the overview it opens from. A cloud-optimised file opens however large it is, as long as those parts fit in 256 MB (a 436 MB EnMAP hyperspectral scene reads about 20 MB, the 1.6 GB NLCD land cover about 14 MB). The parts read are what a saved project keeps. A file that isn't cloud-optimised (in strips, or without overviews) needs most of itself, and past 256 MB the web app says to open it in the desktop app.

With a raster layer selected in Layers, the Style and Data tabs show its groups:

Tab › Group Controls Style › Visibility Range, Effects Scale range, transparency Style › Rendering Symbology: Stretch, RGB, Classify, Unique Values, Colormap, Shaded Relief; Stretch Type: None, Minimum Maximum, Percent Clip, Standard Deviation, Histogram Equalize; DRA (stretch the pixels in view); Resampling (nearest or bilinear); Band Combination (natural colour, colour infrared, or any bands) Style › Enhancement Brightness, contrast, gamma Data Raster information (size, bands, statistics, coordinate system) and Export Raster (GeoTIFF)

Clicking a raster with the Explore tool shows its pixel values. Projects remember a raster's file path and reopen it; rasters added in the browser are stored inside the project.

items.title: Zarr stores
items.text:
Home › Add Data › Zarr… (layer.addZarr) adds a variable of a Zarr store (format 2 or 3), the multidimensional arrays climate and Earth-observation data are kept in: give the store's web address, or (on the desktop) its folder, and Connect lists its variables (raster.zarrInfo). A variable's map is its latitude/longitude (or y/x) dimensions; its other dimensions, such as time or pressure level, are picked a step at a time with a slider, labelled by their coordinates (CF time units as dates, the noleap and 360_day model calendars included). Add to Map adds that step as a raster layer named after the variable and step (tas 2014-07-15), and the dialog stays open to add others. Only the chunks the step needs are fetched, a few at a time, in the background.

Stores are read in pure Rust, in the web app as well as on the desktop: Zarr 2 with consolidated metadata (.zmetadata, as xarray writes) and Zarr 3 (zarr.json, sharded arrays too), chunks compressed with blosc (LZ4, zlib or zstd, byte- or bit-shuffled), zlib, gzip, zstd or LZ4, of integer or float values, in C or Fortran order. A sharded array's shards are fetched whole. _FillValue, missing_value and a Zarr 2 array's fill value are no data; a Zarr 3 array's fill value isn't: chunks never written are left empty, but chunks missing from inside a shard show the fill value. scale_factor and add_offset are applied. The coordinates must be evenly spaced (a curvilinear grid isn't read); longitude/latitude grids of 0–360° are turned to -180–180°, and projected ones take their coordinate system from the variable's grid mapping (crs_wkt, spatial_ref, an EPSG code) or "crs". Blosclz-compressed and transposed chunks and shards inside shards aren't read yet, and say so. A store by web address must allow the browser to fetch it (CORS) for the web app; Google Cloud's CMIP6 bucket does, ARCO-ERA5's doesn't (the desktop reads both).

rustgis-cli run --cmd 'layer.addZarr={"url":"https://storage.googleapis.com/gcp-public-data-arco-era5/ar/1959-2022-full_37-1h-0p25deg-chunk-1.zarr-v2","variable":"2m_temperature","index":{"time":539100}}'

A store in a folder is saved in the project by its folder and slice (2m_temperature[time=539100]) and read again when the project opens, as Add Data on the folder does (its first variable); a store by web address is kept in the project as the slice read. ?zarr=<address> in a web app link opens the dialog on a store.

items.title: Project items
items.text:
RustGIS saves pieces of a project as files you can share and reuse:

Item Extension Made with Opened with Map file (a map with its data) .rgismap Publish › Save As › Map File Home › Import Layer file (a layer with its symbology) .rgislyr Publish › Save As › Layer File Add Data Styles (saved symbology) .rgisstyle Style › Styles › New Style, then Publish › Save As › Style Items Style › Styles › Add Style File Color ramps .rgisramp (also reads QGIS .xml/.qml, GDAL color .txt and GMT .cpt) Publish › Save As › Color Ramps, or by hand Style › Styles › Add Color Ramp File Project template (the setup without features) .rgistemplate Home › Templates, or Publish › Save As Home › Templates › Open Custom Template Project package (everything, rasters included) .rgispkg Publish › Package › Project Project › Open, or drop it on the window Map package / mobile map package .rgismpk Publish › Package › Map or Mobile Map Home › Import Results package (geoprocessing history and outputs) .rgisgpk Publish › Package › Results any zip tool Task (guided command steps) .rgistask Home › Task, Publish › Save As › Task Item Home › Task › Import Task Bookmarks (as longitude, latitude and scale) .rgisbookmarks Home › Navigate › Bookmarks › Export Bookmarks Home › Navigate › Bookmarks › Import Bookmarks Layout .rgislayout Publish › Save Layout File Home › New Layout › Import Layout

Packages are zip files. A mobile map package keeps only the visible layers and simplifies their geometry, for phones and tablets. Styles can also be imported from the layers of a layer file, map file or project. Data › Layer Templates adds empty layers with ready-made schemas (places, routes, areas, observations…) to draw into. Add Folder connects a folder to the Browser, which also lists the project's layouts, styles and tasks. A task's steps each run a command; New Task From History turns the geoprocessing history into a task you can replay.

items.title: Creating features
items.text: Edit › Create draws new points, lines and polygons into the layer selected in Layers: click each vertex and double-click to finish (Esc cancels). Delete (Del) removes the selected features. Edit attributes in the attribute table (Ctrl+T): double-click a cell to change it. Data › Data Design (and Data › Fields) adds and deletes fields and calculates a field from an expression; Calculate Geometry fills a field with each feature's area, length or coordinates. Every edit is one undo step.

items.title: Modifying features
items.text:
The Edit tab's Edit button turns editing on or off for the map; with it off, the map is read-only. The Editing pane (Settings, Templates, Status, Modify) holds the rest:

  • Modify: move the selected features by metres east and north, rotate them, scale them, merge them (polygons are unioned), explode multipart features, split a line where you click, and flip line direction. Edit › Tools lists every editing tool.
  • Feature templates: named default values for new features, made from a selected feature; the Create tool uses the chosen template.
  • Snapping: new vertices snap to nearby vertices, edges and line ends (magenta marker).
  • Elevation: new features get a z value, constant or sampled from a raster surface.
  • Ground to grid: a scale factor and rotation applied to entered distances and directions (Move, and edit.traverse, which draws a line or polygon from distances and bearings).
  • Topology: rules (must not overlap, must not have gaps, must not self-intersect, must not have dangles, must be covered by); Validate lists the errors, and clicking one zooms to it.
  • Status: features added, changed and deleted per layer since the last save.

items.title: Data design
items.text:
The Data tab's Data Design pane keeps attributes valid, on every edit (creating, pasting, attribute edits, Calculate Field):

  • Domains: coded values (code=description) or a numeric range for a field.
  • Subtypes: an integer field's codes, each with a name and default values for new features; the layer is symbolized by subtype.
  • Attribute rules: calculations (a field set from an expression on every insert and update) and constraints (a SQL condition every feature must meet).
  • Contingent values: the combinations of values allowed across fields.
  • Archiving: keeps every edit with its time; restore the layer as it was minutes ago.
  • Relationships: link two layers by key fields; Related Data selects the rows related to the selection.

items.title: Clipboard and pop-ups
items.text:
Copy (Ctrl+C) and Cut (Ctrl+X) take the selected features. Paste (Ctrl+V) adds them to the layer selected in Layers, matching fields by name; Paste Special adds them as a new layer. Copied features also go on the system clipboard as GeoJSON, so they can be pasted into another RustGIS window or a text editor, and GeoJSON copied elsewhere pastes into RustGIS. Copy Path copies the selected layer's data source path.

Pop-ups (Home › Navigate) choose which layers a click with Explore identifies: the topmost layer under the click, every visible layer, only selectable layers, only the layer selected in Layers, or nothing. The pop-up lists every feature under the click in those layers, overlapping ones included (up to 100): step through them with ‹ ›. The feature shown is the one selected. The magnifier in the pop-up's header zooms to it.

items.title: Layouts
items.text:
Home › New Layout adds a page layout (Letter to A0, landscape or portrait) with a map frame, title, legend, north arrow, scale bar and a dynamic credits line. Layouts open as tabs next to the maps; while one is open, its groups lead the Publish tab:

  • Map frames: rectangle, circle and ellipse frames, or polygon and lasso frames drawn on the page. Each frame shows a map of the project at its own centre and scale. Turn on Pan/Zoom Map (Map Frames group, or a frame's properties) to drag inside frames to pan their maps and turn the wheel to zoom them about the pointer; Esc turns it off. Without it, Shift-drag a frame to pan its map. Double-click a frame to match the map view, or set the scale in its properties. Grid draws a labelled graticule over a frame; Extent Indicator outlines another frame's extent (an overview map).
  • Map surrounds: north arrow, scale bar, legend, table frame (a layer's attribute table) and chart frame (a bar chart of a numeric field), plus a neatline or backdrop. A legend shows what its frame draws: only layers with a feature at the frame's scale (through their definition query, display filters and scale range) and, for Unique Values, only the classes those features have, with <all other values> only when some feature falls in it and its symbol is not fully transparent. Graduated Colors and Proportional Symbols list their classes as they are (they are taken from the kept features when the symbology is applied). A layer that draws nothing there, such as an empty one, is left out, in layouts saved before this too. Tick All classes in its properties ("allClasses": true) to list every class of every visible layer instead, and Hide other values ("hideOther": true) to leave <all other values> out of the legend in either mode (the features it stands for are still drawn).
  • Text and Dynamic Text: {date}, {time}, {scale}, {map}, {crs}, {page}, {pages}, {pageName} and {layout} fill in when the page is drawn. Picture places a PNG or JPEG.
  • Map Series: one page per feature of an index layer, with the frame zoomed to each feature; step through pages, refresh, and export every page into one PDF.
  • Click an element to select it, drag to move, drag its handles to resize, and edit it in the properties panel. The wheel zooms the page.
  • Rulers and guides: rulers along the top and left show millimetres from the page's corner. Drag out of a ruler to add a guide, drag a guide to move it, and drag it back onto a ruler to remove it. Guides are saved with the layout but never printed or exported. Clear Guides removes them all, and Rulers in the Page group hides the rulers.
  • Snap: a dragged or resized element snaps to the guides, the page's edges and centre, and the other elements' edges and centres, and the line it snapped to is highlighted. Hold Alt to place an element freely, or turn Snap off in the Page group.
  • Export writes PDF (every map series page) or PNG; Print opens the PDF in the system viewer; Save Layout File and Import Layout move layouts between projects (.rgislayout).

items.title: Reports
items.text:
Publish › New Report lists the selected layer's records page after page; the Report pane previews it and sets it up.

  • Data: pick the detail Fields (or Autofill Fields), Group records by up to four fields (each group gets a heading and its own statistics), add Statistics (count, sum, mean, minimum, maximum), a Dynamic Picture per record (a field holding a PNG/JPEG path relative to the saved project's folder, or base64 image data), Attachments (a field listing each record's files, separated by ;; image files show when they're inside the project's folder), and a Chart Frame (records, or a field's sum, per category).
  • Report Section: Supplemental Pages of text before or after the records, New Template and Existing Template (a page layout drawn as a report page), a Related Report appended after this one, and Subreports (each record's related records through a relationship, listed beneath it).
  • A where clause or the layer's selection limits the records; a sort field orders them within their groups.
  • Publish › Report: Export Report writes a PDF (or the first page as PNG); Save As Report File keeps the report, and Report Template its design without the data source, to start reports on other layers (Publish › Import Report).

items.title: Presentations and notebooks
items.text:
Publish › New Presentation starts a presentation with a title page; the Presentation pane previews, edits and plays it.

  • Page: a Map page shows the map view as it is now, a Blank page shows text on a coloured page, an Image page a picture with a caption, and a Video page a video file or URL with an optional poster picture.
  • Each page has a title, speaker notes and a duration (for Play), and can move up or down.
  • Publish › Presentation › Export Presentation writes a self-contained HTML slideshow (arrow keys, N for notes, P to play; videos play in place), a PDF, or the first page as PNG. Save As Presentation File keeps it to import into other projects.

Analyze › New Notebook starts a notebook of text and command cells; Add and Open opens a RustGIS (.rgisnb) or Jupyter (.ipynb) notebook. A command cell runs one command per line (id {json}, as in scripts) and shows each command's result beneath it. Notebooks save in either format.

items.title: Maps and Basemaps
items.text: A project holds one or more maps (Home › New Map), each with its own layers, basemap, projection, bookmarks and view settings. Maps open as tabs above the map view.

items.title: Navigating
items.text:
Drag to pan and scroll to zoom; Home (or Full Extent) shows all the data. Map › Navigate has fixed zoom steps, Previous and Next extents, Bookmarks (the World Atlas has World, Europe, Africa, Americas and East Asia) and Go To XY, which pans to a longitude and latitude. New Bookmark… saves the current view under a name, with an optional description of the place. The Bookmarks menu removes a bookmark with the button beside it, and exports or imports them as a .rgisbookmarks file. Imported bookmarks show the same place on a map in another projection; places that projection can't show are skipped. Type a scale in the status bar to jump to it. More navigation tools are under View effects below.

Manage Bookmarks (at the foot of the Bookmarks menu, or View › Windows › Bookmarks) opens the Bookmarks pane: every map's bookmarks, grouped by map (the map in view in the accent colour), with a box that filters them by name or description. On each bookmark, Zoom To shows its place at its scale and Pan To centres it at the current scale; a bookmark of another map takes the map in view to the same place. Update saves the current view into it (only on its own map, in view), and Delete removes it. The chevron shows its description: click it to write or edit it. Double-click a name to rename it, and right-click it to rename, describe, update, move it up or down, or delete it. Everything the pane does is a bookmark.* command and undoes with Ctrl+Z.

Find Place (map.findPlace) looks up a place or an address by name with OpenStreetMap's Nominatim (or a Photon server, or a geocoder of your own given by its address) and zooms to the one picked. The search goes to that server over the network; see Geocoding addresses for whole tables.

The search box at the foot of the left pane searches the map as you type: a latitude and longitude (40.7, -74.0, 40.7N 74W or 40°42'46"N 74°0'21"W; latitude first unless the letters or a number past ±90 say otherwise), the map's layers and bookmarks by name, and the values in its layers' attribute tables (the best few per layer, by the feature's name where it has one). Places come from Nominatim when you press Enter on Search places, since the public servers don't allow searching as you type. The arrow keys move through the list and Enter picks: a layer is zoomed to, a feature selected and zoomed to, and a coordinate or a place is marked with a pin until the box is cleared (✕ or Esc). map.search runs the same search from the command line or a script, and goes to a hit with "go":

rustgis-cli run --sample --cmd 'map.search={"query":"Tokyo","go":true}'

Right-click the map for a menu about that place. Its first row shows the latitude and longitude; click it to copy them. Below it, Copy As GeoJSON copies the place as a point feature, Center Map Here and Zoom In Here move the view, and Directions To Here and Directions From Here open the Directions pane. Quick Analysis runs a tool at the place: a buffer of 500 m, 1 km or 5 km (¼, 1 or 5 miles when the Directions pane is set to miles; gp.bufferPoint), a viewshed of 2, 5 or 15 km or a line of sight on an elevation raster in the map, and Open In Geoprocessing… opens the Buffer tool. View In Google Maps and View In Google Earth open the place in your browser at about the same zoom.

items.title: Directions
items.text:
Directions (Home › Navigate) plans a route between places and follows it turn by turn, with the public Valhalla server run by FOSSGIS on OpenStreetMap data. Pick Drive, Bike or Walk, then set the start and the destination: type an address (Enter looks it up with Nominatim) or a latitude and longitude, press the ⌖ button and click the map, or right-click the map and choose Directions From Here or Directions To Here. + Add Stop adds places on the way (up to 20 in all), Swap reverses the trip, and a drive can avoid tolls, highways or ferries; Miles gives distances in miles and feet.

Routes are drawn as soon as every place is set. Between two places the server offers up to two other ways, drawn grey: pick one in the list or click it on the map. The steps list each maneuver with its arrow, instruction and distance; click one to zoom to it. Simulate replays the route as a drive the map follows, with the next maneuver and its distance in a banner across the top of the map, at 1× to 16× speed (pause, drag the slider to jump along, End to stop). Save as Layer adds the route as a line layer, and its maneuvers as a point layer, to style, export (GPX, GeoJSON…) or keep with the project.

The first time, the pane asks before anything is sent: planning a route sends its places to the routing server, and looking a place up sends its name to Nominatim. Travel times don't include live traffic, and the public server is shared, so it answers light use only.

map.route plans a route from the command line, a script or the AI Assistant, with places given as [lon, lat], "lat, lon" or a name to look up, and adds it and its steps as layers; ui.pane.directions with from, to (and via, mode) opens the pane on a route. map.route sends its places to the same public servers (names to Nominatim, at most five a call, a second apart; coordinates to FOSSGIS's Valhalla), so the AI Assistant asks before running it:

rustgis-cli run --sample --cmd 'map.route={"from":"Brandenburg Gate, Berlin","to":"Alexanderplatz, Berlin","mode":"bike"}'

items.title: Basemaps
items.text:
Home › Add › Basemap offers five built-in basemaps drawn from a world outline (Paper, Midnight, Ocean, Atlas, Blank), which need no network, and web tile layers over them:

  • Raster tiles from an XYZ or TMS template (https://…/{z}/{x}/{y}.png; {-y} for rows from the south, {s} for subdomains, {q} for Bing-style quadkeys) or a WMS through {bbox-epsg-3857}. PNG, JPEG and WebP.
  • Vector tiles (Mapbox Vector Tiles, .pbf) from a template or a TileJSON address, drawn in a built-in style that knows the OpenMapTiles, Protomaps and Shortbread schemas.
  • PMTiles archives (.pmtiles) of raster or vector tiles: a web address, read a tile at a time by byte ranges (the server must allow range requests, and CORS for the web app), or on the desktop a file (Tile Archive File…, Add Data, or drop it on the window). A vector archive that is a basemap is drawn in the built-in style; any other is drawn with each of its layers in a colour of its own.
  • MBTiles files (.mbtiles) of raster or vector tiles, drawn as PMTiles archives are: on the desktop read in place a tile at a time (Tile Archive File…, Add Data, or drop it on the window); in the web app added with Add Data and held in memory for the session (a project keeps the layer, and asks for the file again).
  • Map styles: a MapLibre style document (style.json), with its vector and raster sources. RustGIS draws background, fill, line, circle and raster layers, point labels with their icons from the style's sprite (SDF icons in their icon-color), and fill patterns; it evaluates the style's expressions and zoom functions. Line labels and shields along roads, line patterns, hillshade and 3D extrusion are not drawn (extrusions draw flat). A label shows the lines of its text that the map's font can draw: a style's "Syria / سوريا" shows as "Syria".

The gallery's Web Basemaps need no API key: the OpenFreeMap vector maps (Liberty, Bright, Positron, Dark, Fiord) and USGS Imagery. Choosing one replaces the other web basemaps. For many more (OpenStreetMap, Esri, NASA and others), follow Install the Basemaps plugin under them, which opens the Plugin Manager at the Basemaps plugin; it adds a tab of public basemaps. Add any other with Add Tile Layer… at the bottom of the Basemap gallery. The gallery lists the map's tile layers: show or hide them, change their opacity and order, or remove them. The Layers pane lists them too, under the map's layers and above the basemap: tick one to show or hide it, and right-click it for its opacity, order and Remove. Overlays (labels, roads) stay on top of the basemaps; choosing a built-in basemap removes the web basemaps but keeps the overlays. Tile layers are saved with the project, and their credits are shown in the corner of the map and drawn on exports.

Tiles load in the background and the map fills in as they arrive, with coarser tiles standing in meanwhile; exports and rustgis-cli wait for them. On the globe and in other projections the tiles are reprojected. From scripts: map.addTiles, map.removeTiles, map.setTiles and map.tiles.

items.title: Worldview
items.text: The world outline and the World Atlas sample's countries come in two worldviews: Natural Earth's default borders, and China's (Natural Earth's China point of view: Taiwan, Aksai Chin and South Tibet are part of China). RustGIS picks China's when the system's time zone is mainland China's (such as Asia/Shanghai) or its first locale is zh-CN; nothing is looked up over the network. Choose one in Settings › Language › Worldview, set RUSTGIS_WORLDVIEW (default or china), or pass --worldview to rustgis-cli. An untouched sample project switches its countries at once; others keep the layer they have.

items.title: Projections
items.text:
The flat map is drawn in Web Mercator by default. View › Projection switches it to another projection, and clicking the coordinate system in the status bar opens the Coordinate System dialog, which also takes a projected EPSG code (such as 3035, 32633 for UTM zone 33N or 2056 for Switzerland). A code whose projection method or datum grid RustGIS can't use (Polyconic such as 5880, Cassini, oblique Mercator, or a NAD27 code that needs a grid) is refused with the reason, rather than drawn in another projection:

Preset Kind Equirectangular, Miller World, cylindrical Mollweide, Lambert Cylindrical Equal Area, Equal Earth, Eckert IV World, equal-area Robinson, Natural Earth, Winkel Tripel World, compromise North / South Polar Stereographic Polar Europe Equal Area (ETRS89 LAEA), USA Contiguous Albers Equal Area Regional, equal-area

Layers are projected on the fly. A feature that crosses the edge of a world projection (the meridian opposite its central one, such as 90°E in Equal Earth Americas) is cut there and drawn on both sides of the map. Each projection has an area of use: polar projections show their hemisphere poleward of 30°, regional ones their region, transverse Mercator (UTM) zones 30° either side of their meridian, and data outside it isn't drawn. Switching keeps the centre and scale, and the choice is saved with the map (map.projection from the command line). A raster already in the map's coordinate system draws without being reprojected. To open every new session in a projection, set it in Settings › Start-up › Projection. Robinson, Equal Earth, Natural Earth, Winkel Tripel and Eckert IV are computed by RustGIS itself on a sphere, so EPSG:8857 (Equal Earth) works too.

items.title: Globe
items.text:
View › Globe shows the map as a 3D globe seen from space instead of the flat Web Mercator map, and back again. Drag to turn the globe, scroll to zoom, and use Full Extent to see the whole Earth. Every layer draws on the globe: vectors are clipped at the horizon and follow great circles, rasters are draped onto the sphere, and labels, selection, identify, measuring and editing work as on the flat map. The scale stays the same when you switch, and the choice is saved with each map in the project (map.projection from the command line).

While the globe turns or zooms, the map is drawn flat once and laid over the sphere by the graphics card, so it moves smoothly whatever the basemap; labels come back, and the map is drawn exactly, as soon as it stops.

The globe hangs in dark space, in the light theme too, with stars around it and now and then a shooting star passing behind it. View › Visual Effect › Stars turns them off (exports show the stars but never the shooting stars).

items.title: View effects
items.text:
The View tab adds effects drawn over the map: Illumination (day and night shading for a time, with twilight), Weather (haze, fog, rain, snow), Visual Effect (vignette, edges, the stars around the globe), Camera Effect (tilt-shift blur, film grain) and Postprocessing (brightness, contrast, saturation, sepia). The Color Vision simulator shows the map as people with protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia or achromatopsia see it (on screen only; exports are untouched).

Global shows a globe; Local a flat view centred where you are (azimuthal equidistant; not in the web app, which doesn't include that projection). Wireframe draws polygons as outlines, Depth Priority lifts a layer above others whatever its order, View Clipping hides features beyond a distance from the centre, and Speed Display draws without antialiasing. The Navigator adds a compass, zoom buttons and a pan pad; Camera shows and sets the position and scale; the Magnifier shows twice the map under the pointer. On the Home tab, First-Person navigation walks with W A S D and flies up and down with Q and E. The interface follows the system's light or dark setting; View › Display › Dark Mode switches it by hand.

View › Display › GPU Rendering (beta) draws the flat map on the GPU instead of the CPU: vector layers are tessellated once and re-projected per frame, so panning and zooming stay smooth on large datasets. It is off by default, and the setting is remembered across sessions (ui.map.gpu is the command; RUSTGIS_GPU=1 forces it on for development). The globe, view effects and the colour-vision simulator always render on the CPU, and exports are unaffected — the choice only changes the on-screen flat map.

items.title: Exporting
items.text:
Publish › Output › Export Map writes the map view as a PNG at any DPI, with labels, the scale bar and tile credits (share.exportMap on the command line); Print Map sends it through the system's PDF viewer, Capture To Clipboard copies it, and Export To 3D writes a layer as a Wavefront OBJ model with polygons extruded by a field. Data › Export (or the Export Features tool) writes a layer to GeoJSON, CSV, GeoPackage, GeoParquet, Shapefile, FlatGeobuf, KML, KMZ or GPX (see Writing), Data › Export a raster to GeoTIFF, and Data Interop converts layers to KML, GPX or CSV with WKT. Layouts, reports and presentations export to PDF from their own tabs and panes (see Layouts and Reports).

Packages and project item files are described under Project items.

items.title: Sharing as open formats
items.text:
Publish › Share As writes open-format files that work without a server, to a chosen file or the first data store (a folder registered under Publish › Manage › Data Stores):

  • Web Map: a self-contained HTML page with the map's layers (rasters as images), pan and zoom, a layer list and pop-ups.
  • Web Layer: the selected layer as a static OGC API – Features collection, with its style and a viewer page, in a zip. Geodata Service does the same for every layer and table.
  • Web Style: the selected layer's symbology as a MapLibre style (unique values and classes as expressions).
  • Locator: the selected layer's names as a place-search file; locator.find searches it and can zoom to the best match.
  • Web Tool: the last model as a tool file, which model.import adds to another project.
  • Web Scene: the map in 3D as glTF, polygons extruded by their layer's extrusion setting.
  • Web Link Chart: the features joined by the map's relationships, as a node-link page.

Status › Jobs (the Shared Items pane) lists every share; Save Web Map, Replace Web Layer, Save Web Scene and Save Web Link Chart update a share in place, and Upload File copies a file into a data store.

items.title: Workspace
items.text:
Tools for working across maps and views, and for setting up the app the way you like it.

  • Side by Side shows a second map beside the active one; Link Views keeps maps at the same place and scale, and Link Cursors marks the pointer's place on the other map.
  • Browser View shows the project's maps, layouts, tables, styles, tasks, models, folders and offline areas as cards (double-click to open); Item Pop-ups add hover details.
  • Pane Sets save the panes you have open and bring them back. Tasks steps through a task's instructions; the Workflow Manager tracks jobs (new, in progress, on hold, done) with the area each covers.
  • Thumbnails for the project and for each map, from the view or an image.
  • Animation: add keyframes (views), play them, and export the moves as PNG frames.
  • Profile: elevation profiles along clicked points or selected lines, auto-completed to the raster's edge, or across a line (a cross section), with gain, loss and a chart.
  • Infographics (Home tab) summarise what's in view: counts, totals and top categories.
  • Offline: Download Map takes the data in view into an offline area; open it to edit, then Sync sends changed, new and deleted features back and refreshes it. Feature Cache prepares every layer's geometry for the current projection (Fill, Empty, Cancel, Auto Cache).
  • Help: choose the ribbon's tabs and the Quick Access Toolbar's buttons, open the user guide, and watch the Diagnostic Monitor (frame rate, draw time, data size).
  • Plugins: Plugins › Plugin Manager installs, updates and removes plugins from the registry at plugins.rustgis.app or from a file.
  • Language: Settings › Language switches the interface among 16 languages and chooses the worldview of the built-in borders.
  • Start-up: Settings › Start-up sets what RustGIS opens with: Start With the World Atlas sample or a blank map, or, in the desktop app, Last Project (the .rgis project last opened or saved) or Choose Project… (one you pick once), the Projection the map opens in (a preset or a supported projected EPSG code, such as 3010), and the Extent it opens on (the full extent, or Use Current View to keep the view you are looking at). A project opened at start keeps its own projection and view; the Projection and Extent settings apply to the sample and a blank map. If the project no longer opens (moved or deleted), RustGIS starts with the sample and says why. After a crash it starts with the sample too, in case the project is what crashed; starting rustgis --sample also skips the start-up project. The choices are remembered on this computer, or in this browser for the web app. Opening files from the command line starts a blank map.
